Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Anthropology: Humans made in God’s image, fallen by Adam’s sin; human beings are mortal (no inherent immortal soul), die unconsciously until resurrection, and are capable of moral choice and sanctification.
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Cosmology: Young‑Earth creationist framework (six literal days), a created universe governed by God, with the ‘great controversy’ theme (Christ vs. Satan) explaining the presence of evil and history’s direction.
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Ecclesiology: Denominational, organized structure with local congregations connected to regional and global bodies (representative governance); emphasis on missionary outreach and institutional life (schools, hospitals, publishing).
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Epistemology: Primacy of Scripture interpreted historically‑grammatically; the prophetic ministry of Ellen G. White is authoritative as a continuing spiritual guide but subordinate to the Bible; reason, experience and tradition inform understanding.
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Eschatology: Historicist and imminent expectation of Christ’s Second Coming, followed by the millennium, the resurrection of the righteous, final judgment and the restoration of a renewed earth; apocalyptic prophecy (Daniel, Revelation) is central.
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Ethics & Morality: Moral life centered on the Ten Commandments and Christlike character: honesty, chastity, temperance, healthful living (often vegetarianism, abstaining from alcohol/tobacco), social responsibility and service.
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Exclusivity: Affirms salvation only in Christ and the universal offer of grace, while holding distinctives (e.g., investigative judgment, Sabbath theology — though this branch observes Sunday) that mark boundary lines; generally evangelistic rather than isolationist.
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Metaphysics: Biblical theism: a personal, triune God who created reality; reality is purposeful and moral, grounded in divine law and a cosmic conflict between good and evil.
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Praxis: Corporate worship, Bible study, prayer, baptism by immersion, Lord’s Supper (often with foot‑washing), evangelism, health and education ministries; in this Sunday‑observing branch corporate worship and Sabbath rest are practiced on Sunday rather than Saturday.
Adventist movement (Sunday observing).Soteriology: Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, evidenced by repentance and obedience; emphasis on sanctification, the tension of faith and works, and distinctive doctrines such as the investigative judgment (historic Adventist teaching).

African traditional religions Ethnic.Anthropology: Human identity is primarily social and relational—defined by kin, lineage, community and roles; personhood is developed and affirmed through rites of passage, responsibilities and reciprocal ties with ancestors and spirits.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Cosmology: A layered, relational cosmos (sky, earth, underworld or spirit realms) in which natural forces and spirits animate the world; time is often cyclical and rituals/rites keep cosmic balance and seasonal order.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Ecclesiology: Religious authority is typically decentralized and embedded in kinship, age‑grades, secret societies and specialist roles; there is no single universal church structure but locally grounded institutions and leaders.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Epistemology: Knowledge comes through oral tradition, myth, divination, dreams, signs and the expertise of elders/initiates; truth is often validated by ritual efficacy and communal consensus rather than abstract proof.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Eschatology: Varied perspectives with emphasis on continuity: the dead may become ancestors, be reborn, or dwell in a spirit realm; less emphasis on cosmic apocalypse or final judgment and more on ongoing relationships across generations.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms prioritize communal welfare, reciprocity, respect for elders and observance of taboos and obligations; ethics are practical, context‑sensitive, and judged by effects on social and cosmic harmony.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Exclusivity: Generally non‑exclusive and syncretic—religious identity is often by birth or initiation and communities may incorporate elements of other religions; certain rituals or societies, however, can be restricted to insiders.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Metaphysics: Many communities posit a Supreme Being alongside a multitude of lesser gods, spirits and ancestors; the material and spiritual realms are interpenetrating and persons are often seen as composites of body, life‑force/soul and social destiny. Beliefs vary widely by group.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Praxis: Religious life emphasizes ritual: offerings, sacrifices, divination, healing, masks, music, dance, sacred places and rites of passage; specialists (priests, diviners, healers) perform and mediate these practices.
African traditional religions Ethnic.Soteriology: Not centered on individual salvation but on restoring and maintaining harmony, health and social order; healing, reconciliation, purification and proper ritual practice are the means to avert misfortune and secure communal well‑being.

Ahl-i Hadith.Anthropology: Humans are God’s created beings, endowed with fitrah (natural disposition), moral responsibility and free will within the framework of divine decree; human dignity and accountability are emphasized rather than doctrines of original sin.
Ahl-i Hadith.Cosmology: Traditional Islamic cosmology: the universe is created by God and populated by angels, jinn and humans; supernatural elements described in the Qur'an and hadith are accepted literally and without allegorizing.
Ahl-i Hadith.Ecclesiology: Non-hierarchical, scholar-centered communities: religious authority rests with learned ulama, imams and study institutions (madrasas) rather than a centralized clergy; local congregations and networks organize communal life.
Ahl-i Hadith.Epistemology: Scripturalist epistemology: the Qur'an and authentic hadith are primary; ijma (consensus) and reasoning are subsidiary, while blind adherence to madhhab taqlid is rejected in favor of direct textual evidence and hadith-criticism.
Ahl-i Hadith.Eschatology: Conventional Sunni eschatology accepted literally: resurrection, judgment, heaven and hell, major and minor signs of the Hour, and traditional accounts of the Mahdi and the return of Jesus (Isa).
Ahl-i Hadith.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms derive from the Qur'an and hadith; emphasis on obedience to sharia, personal piety, modesty, social duties and rejection of practices seen as bid'ah (religious innovation).
Ahl-i Hadith.Exclusivity: Self-understood as a movement to restore pure, text-based Islam, thus often critical of Sufi practices, popular devotional forms and strict madrasa-centered taqlid; stresses doctrinal purity though attitudes toward other Muslims vary by group and context.
Ahl-i Hadith.Metaphysics: Absolute monotheism (tawhid): God is unique, transcendent and sovereign; divine attributes are affirmed as stated in scripture without speculative theological interpretation (Athari/textualist orientation).
Ahl-i Hadith.Praxis: Strict observance of the five pillars and hadith-prescribed ritual forms, communal prayer and simple, textually grounded worship; rejection of many Sufi rites, saint veneration and local innovations in ritual.
Ahl-i Hadith.Soteriology: Salvation is through correct belief (iman) and righteous deeds, repentance and adherence to the Qur'an and authentic Sunnah; following revealed guidance and avoiding innovations are central to being rightly guided.

Anglican.Anthropology: Human beings are made in the image of God (imago Dei), endowed with dignity and freedom but marred by sin; vocation includes worship, community, and responsible care for creation. Anthropology balances personal responsibility, corporate sin, and the promise of restoration in Christ.
Anglican.Cosmology: The world is God's created, ordered, and good cosmos, now fallen and sustained by divine providence; creation is seen as meaningful and sacramental, revealing God and calling for stewardship. There is no single scientific stance tied to Anglicanism, but a general openness to dialogue between faith and science.
Anglican.Ecclesiology: A historic, apostolic Church expressed in a national and global communion; episcopal polity with bishops, clergy, and laity, holding to the creeds and the sacraments as marks of the Church. The Anglican Communion is a fellowship of autonomous provinces bound by common heritage, not a centralized magisterium.
Anglican.Epistemology: Authority rests on a triad: Scripture primary, interpreted in light of Tradition and informed by Reason (the classical Anglican 'three‑legged stool'), with experience also playing a pastoral role. Doctrinal development is negotiated by synods, bishops, and learned theological reflection.
Anglican.Eschatology: Christian hope in the resurrection of the dead, final judgment, and the renewal of creation (new heavens and new earth); liturgy and sacramental life already anticipate God's kingdom. Specific timelines and millennial views vary widely among Anglicans.
Anglican.Ethics & Morality: Moral life is grounded in Scripture interpreted through tradition and reason, shaped by the creeds, commandments, and the example of Christ; virtues, social justice, and pastoral discernment are central. On many contemporary issues, Anglicans exhibit a range of conclusions arrived at by communal discernment.
Anglican.Exclusivity: Affirms Jesus Christ as the definitive revelation and means of salvation while displaying a range of stances on who is saved—from more particularist claims about Christ's unique mediatorship to broadly hopeful or inclusivist positions recognizing God's mercy beyond visible church boundaries. Pastoral humility and diversity of opinion are common.
Anglican.Metaphysics: Classical Christian realism: one personal Triune God (Father, Son, Spirit) who creates and sustains a real material and spiritual order; incarnation and sacraments underscore the unity of the visible and invisible realms. Emphases and theological vocabulary vary across Evangelical, Broad, and Anglo‑Catholic wings.
Anglican.Praxis: Corporate, liturgical worship centered on the Book of Common Prayer (or local liturgies), with two primary sacraments (Baptism and Eucharist) and other rites (ordination, marriage, funerals). Parish ministry, pastoral care, preaching, education, and social action are key practices.
Anglican.Soteriology: Salvation is by God's grace through Jesus Christ, normally received in faith and lived out in repentance, baptism, and the life of the Church; Anglicanism emphasizes both justification and ongoing sanctification. Practical emphases vary—from Evangelical focus on personal conversion to Anglo‑Catholic stress on sacramental participation as means of grace.

Armenian Apostolic Church.Anthropology: Humans are body and soul, created in the image of God, wounded by sin but capable of restoration and deification (theosis) through communion with God in the Church.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Cosmology: A created, good and ordered cosmos sustained by God; the world fell into disorder through sin and is being restored and sanctified by Christ’s redemptive work.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Ecclesiology: An autocephalous, apostolic church (Armenian Apostolic Church) headed by the Catholicos, organized episcopally with priests and deacons; tightly linked to Armenian national and cultural identity while claiming apostolic origins.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Epistemology: Knowledge of God is mediated by divine revelation—Scripture, Holy Tradition, liturgy, patristic interpretation and the sacraments—with ecclesial authority exercised through bishops in apostolic succession.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Eschatology: Affirms Christ’s second coming, the resurrection of the dead, final judgment and eternal life or separation from God; emphasizes hope of participation in God’s life and prays for the departed.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Ethics & Morality: Moral teaching rooted in Scripture, the teachings of the Fathers and liturgical life: love of God and neighbor, charity, virtue, confession, fasting and ascetic disciplines shaping personal and communal holiness.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Exclusivity: Claims apostolic continuity and the fullness of sacramental life in its tradition; historically distinct from Chalcedonian churches (Oriental Orthodox identity) and not always in full communion with them, though modern dialogues stress substantial shared faith.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Metaphysics: Classical Christian theism: one Triune God; Jesus Christ is the incarnate Word. The Armenian Church holds an Oriental Orthodox (miaphysite) Christology—one united divine-human nature in Christ—and affirms the reality of sacraments and divine grace.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Praxis: Centered on the Badarak (Divine Liturgy) and a sacramental rhythm (traditionally seven sacraments), regular fasting and feast cycles, veneration of saints and icons, monasticism and parish ministry.
Armenian Apostolic Church.Soteriology: Salvation comes through Christ’s incarnation, death and resurrection and is received by faith, repentance and participation in the Church’s sacramental life (baptism, Eucharist, etc.), prayer and ascetic practice, oriented toward union with God.

Baptist.Anthropology: Humans are created in God's image, possess moral agency and personhood, are fallen into sin and spiritually dependent on God for restoration.
Baptist.Cosmology: God created the universe (often held ex nihilo), sustains it by providence, and the world is good but affected by the Fall and awaiting redemption.
Baptist.Ecclesiology: Congregational polity with local church autonomy and the priesthood of all believers; membership by profession of faith and believer's baptism; voluntary associations and conventions for cooperative work.
Baptist.Epistemology: Primacy of Scripture (sola scriptura) as the ultimate authority, interpreted by the individual believer under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, with reason and tradition playing secondary roles.
Baptist.Eschatology: Diverse views (premillennial, dispensational, amillennial, postmillennial among others) but commonly affirm Christ's second coming, bodily resurrection, final judgment, heaven and hell.
Baptist.Ethics & Morality: Moral guidance derives primarily from Scripture; emphasis on personal holiness, family and sexual ethics, and social responsibility—specific positions vary widely among Baptist bodies.
Baptist.Exclusivity: Generally exclusivist in soteriology: salvation is through faith in Christ alone; vigorous evangelistic impulse and historic commitment to religious liberty and voluntary faith commitments.
Baptist.Metaphysics: Classical Trinitarian Christian theism: one God in three persons who is personal, transcendent and immanent; reality includes created persons (souls), angels and demons, and moral order grounded in God.
Baptist.Praxis: Worship centers on preaching, Scripture reading and congregational singing; two ordinances—believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper; strong focus on evangelism, missions and discipleship.
Baptist.Soteriology: Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ alone; regeneration and repentance accompany saving faith; believer's baptism is an ordinance that publicly marks conversion but is not generally seen as the means of salvation.

Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Anthropology: Humans are spirit-soul-body composites who are fallen or imperfect but capable of transformation; true human fulfillment comes through spiritual rebirth and alignment with divine life as taught by the movement.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Cosmology: A spiritual cosmology in which a transcendent God created the visible and invisible worlds; existence is ordered by a struggle between divine order (embodied by the Cross and Star symbolism) and spiritual disorder or evil forces.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Ecclesiology: Highly organized, leader-centered fellowship with an international network of branches; institutional authority is concentrated in the movement's central leadership and its interpretation of doctrine and practice.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Epistemology: Authoritative revelation combines the Bible with continuing, charismatic revelation centered on the founder and the Brotherhood's leadership; spiritual experience, prophecy and the founder's teachings are primary sources of truth.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Eschatology: Expectation of an ultimate transformation of humanity and society under divine rule—often framed as the coming or realization of the Kingdom of God through the Brotherhood's spiritual program and leadership.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Ethics & Morality: Emphasizes holiness, obedience, love, peace and strict moral discipline in personal and social life; members are expected to live apart from certain secular practices and to model high standards of conduct.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Exclusivity: Generally exclusivist: the Brotherhood presents itself as the true vehicle of divine truth and salvation, holding that authentic spiritual restoration is found within its community and teachings.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Metaphysics: Monotheistic but incarnational: God is supreme and is believed by followers to have uniquely manifested in the person of the movement's founder (Olumba Olumba Obu). Reality is fundamentally spiritual, with moral and mystical forces shaping human destiny.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Praxis: Regular communal worship, prayer, teaching, healing and faith practices under the movement's rites and leadership; distinctive dress and behavioral codes and active communal life/mission characterize daily practice.
Brotherhood of the Cross and Star.Soteriology: Salvation is attained through recognition of and union with the divine manifestation in the founder, adherence to the Brotherhood's teachings and moral discipline, and participation in its spiritual life; redemption is both personal and communal.

Buddhist.Anthropology: Persons are composite, impermanent processes (five aggregates/skandhas) rather than enduring souls; identity and continuity are karmic and conditioned flow of mind and matter.
Buddhist.Cosmology: A cyclical, multilayered cosmos of rebirth realms (gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, hells) governed by karma, with no single eternal creator; worlds arise and pass through cosmic cycles.
Buddhist.Ecclesiology: No centralized universal church; the sangha (monastic community) is foundational, supported by diverse lay communities and many autonomous schools and lineages.
Buddhist.Epistemology: Knowledge is validated by direct meditative insight, scriptural study, reason, and teacher transmission; emphasis on experiential verification ('come and see').
Buddhist.Eschatology: No single apocalyptic finale—history is cyclical and individual rebirth continues until awakening; emphasis is on liberation from the cycle rather than a final end-time.
Buddhist.Ethics & Morality: Ethics center on intention and karmic consequences: compassion, non-harming, and observance of precepts (e.g., five precepts) guide conduct and reduce suffering.
Buddhist.Exclusivity: Tends toward pragmatic pluralism and compatibility with other beliefs; most traditions are non-exclusive though some schools assert doctrinal superiority.
Buddhist.Metaphysics: Reality is characterized by impermanence (anicca), non-self (anatta), and dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); ultimate reality is often described in terms of emptiness (śūnyatā) rather than a permanent substance or creator deity.
Buddhist.Praxis: Includes meditation practices (insight/vipassanā, concentration/samatha), monastic discipline, devotional rituals, chanting, and ethical training tailored by tradition and culture.
Buddhist.Soteriology: Liberation (nirvāṇa/enlightenment) is attained by extinguishing craving and ignorance through ethical conduct, meditation, and wisdom; schools differ on path ideals (arhat vs. bodhisattva).

Byzantine Rite.Anthropology: Humans are made in the image and likeness of God; the Fall wounded but did not annihilate the image. The goal of human life is theosis—participation in divine life—affecting both body and soul.
Byzantine Rite.Cosmology: A hierarchically ordered, created cosmos populated by angels and humans; matter is capable of bearing divine presence because the Incarnation sanctified creation. History is the arena of salvation and restoration.
Byzantine Rite.Ecclesiology: The Church is the incarnate Body of Christ: apostolic, sacramental, conciliar, and hierarchical, expressed in local/autocephalous churches under bishops. Unity is primarily liturgical and mystical as well as institutional.
Byzantine Rite.Epistemology: Knowledge of God rests on Scripture, Holy Tradition, the Fathers, and lived liturgical experience. Emphasizes apophatic theology and hesychastic/experiential acquaintance with God via uncreated energies.
Byzantine Rite.Eschatology: Already/not-yet: the Kingdom of God is present in the sacraments but will be fully realized at Christ's second coming—general resurrection, final judgment, and the transfiguration of persons and cosmos into eternal communion with God.
Byzantine Rite.Ethics & Morality: Virtue-centered and relational: imitation of Christ, love of God and neighbor, humility, repentance, and ascetic practice. Moral life is oriented toward transformation into Christlikeness and communion.
Byzantine Rite.Exclusivity: Normatively salvation is mediated by the Church and its sacraments, yet tradition affirms God's mercy and does not dogmatically exclude the possibility of salvation outside visible boundaries; ecclesial membership remains the normative path.
Byzantine Rite.Metaphysics: God is transcendent and personal; the created world is real and good. Divine essence is ultimately inaccessible but communicates itself by uncreated energies (Palamite insight); sacramental realism and the theological role of icons as windows to the divine.
Byzantine Rite.Praxis: Liturgy-centered communal life: Divine Liturgy and the Mysteries (sacraments), veneration of icons, liturgical cycle and fasting, prayer (including the Jesus Prayer), and monastic disciplines.
Byzantine Rite.Soteriology: Salvation is therapeutic: healing, restoration, and deification (theosis). Achieved by synergy of divine grace and human cooperation through repentance, sacraments, prayer, ascetic struggle, and virtue.

Catholic.Anthropology: Human beings are body-soul unities made in the image of God (imago Dei), wounded by original sin yet endowed with reason, free will, and a vocation to communion with God and others.
Catholic.Cosmology: The cosmos is a purposeful creation ordered by God's providence toward communion with Him; spiritual beings (angels, demons) and a teleological hierarchy of creation are affirmed.
Catholic.Ecclesiology: The Church is the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Body of Christ with apostolic succession through bishops and the pope as successor of Peter; the Church is the visible sacramental means of salvation and mission.
Catholic.Epistemology: Sources of knowledge of God are Scripture, Apostolic Tradition, and the Church's Magisterium, integrated with reason and philosophical inquiry; doctrine can develop under authoritative interpretation.
Catholic.Eschatology: History moves toward Christ's return, the resurrection of the body, particular and final judgment, the fulfillment of the kingdom in a new creation; destiny includes heaven, hell, and purification (purgatory) for some.
Catholic.Ethics & Morality: Moral teaching rests on natural law illuminated by divine revelation; objective moral norms, the virtues, human dignity, and the common good guide personal and social ethics.
Catholic.Exclusivity: The Catholic Church claims to possess the fullness of means of salvation and truth, while teaching that salvation is ultimately God’s to mediate and may be available, by His mercy, to those outside visible membership under certain conditions.
Catholic.Metaphysics: Reality is rooted in a personal, triune God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit); created being participates in God's being through grace; sacramental realism holds that material signs can truly convey divine grace.
Catholic.Praxis: Core practices include the Eucharistic liturgy (Mass), seven sacraments, prayer (liturgical and devotional), confession, charitable works, religious life, and observance of the liturgical year.
Catholic.Soteriology: Salvation is won by Christ's life, death, and resurrection and applied through grace; faith and baptism initiate salvation, sanctification proceeds via cooperation with grace, sacraments, and good works within the Church.

Chinese traditional religion.Anthropology: Humans are relational beings embedded in family, lineage, and community, constituted by qi and moral obligation; identity and personhood are defined by roles, duties, and continuing ties with ancestors rather than autonomous individualism.
Chinese traditional religion.Cosmology: Cosmic order is cyclical and relational: the cosmos is a harmonized field of qi shaped by yin-yang dynamics and the Five Phases, with correspondence between Heaven, Earth, and humanity; ritual and moral action maintain cosmic balance.
Chinese traditional religion.Ecclesiology: Decentralized and plural: no single authoritative church. Religious life is organized around family lineage halls, local temples, guilds, and networks of ritual specialists (Daoist priests, mediums, masters) with overlapping civic and ritual roles.
Chinese traditional religion.Epistemology: Knowledge is practical, traditional, and analogical—derived from classical texts, ritual efficacy, divination, observation of patterns and correspondences, and experiential transmission through families and masters rather than abstract theological proof.
Chinese traditional religion.Eschatology: Varied and often non-linear: emphasis on ancestor continuity, ghost and spirit realms, and cycles of rebirth (especially where Buddhist influence exists); ultimate endings or final judgment are generally subsidiary to ongoing maintenance of ancestral and communal ties.
Chinese traditional religion.Ethics & Morality: Ethics emphasize filial piety, ritual propriety (li), social hierarchies, reciprocity, and harmony; moral worth is judged by maintenance of relationships, role-appropriate behavior, and contribution to communal and cosmic balance.
Chinese traditional religion.Exclusivity: Generally non‑exclusive and highly syncretic—individuals commonly combine Confucian, Daoist, Buddhist, and popular folk practices without strict doctrinal boundaries; religious pluralism and pragmatic borrowing are typical.
Chinese traditional religion.Metaphysics: A largely immanent, pluralistic worldview in which qi (vital energy), ancestral and local spirits, numerous gods, and impersonal principles such as Tian (Heaven) and the Dao (Way) coexist; reality is characterized by interpenetrating forces (yin-yang, Five Phases) rather than a single transcendent creator.
Chinese traditional religion.Praxis: A diverse repertoire of rituals and practices: ancestral worship, temple rites, festivals, divination (e.g., I Ching, lots), talismans, feng shui, spirit-mediumship, and Daoist liturgy—performed by families, temples, and ritual specialists to manage luck and social order.
Chinese traditional religion.Soteriology: There is no single doctrine of salvation; aims are pragmatic and communal—harmonizing with the Dao, securing longevity and prosperity, averting misfortune, and sustaining ancestral wellbeing; Daoist practices may seek immortality, while Buddhist influences add notions of karmic liberation.

Church of Sweden.Anthropology: Humans made in the image of God (imago Dei), social and embodied beings who are fallen into sin yet capable of receiving and living out God's grace and vocation.
Church of Sweden.Cosmology: The world is God's creation, upheld by divine providence; creation is ordered, good, but affected by sin and awaits renewal in God's future restoration.
Church of Sweden.Ecclesiology: An episcopal, national Lutheran church with synodal governance: the Church is the community of baptized, organized around parishes, sacraments and ordained ministry, and engaged ecumenically.
Church of Sweden.Epistemology: Scripture as primary authority read in light of the Lutheran confessions, with reason, tradition and experience informing theological reflection and preaching.
Church of Sweden.Eschatology: Centered on Christ's resurrection, final judgment and the hope of new creation; emphasis on Christian hope and ethical living rather than detailed apocalyptic speculation.
Church of Sweden.Ethics & Morality: Grounded in Scripture and Christian teaching: love of God and neighbor, justice, care for the vulnerable; interpreted through a Lutheran two-kingdom awareness and a modern emphasis on human rights, equality and social responsibility.
Church of Sweden.Exclusivity: Affirms Christ as the unique Savior in doctrine but practices ecumenical openness and inclusivity—welcoming other Christians, engaging in dialogue, and emphasizing pastoral breadth rather than strict doctrinal exclusivism.
Church of Sweden.Metaphysics: Classical Christian/Trinitarian: one God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) who is transcendent and immanent; created reality is real and good and bears sacramental significance.
Church of Sweden.Praxis: Liturgical worship shaped by the church year, preaching, infant baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, pastoral care and diaconal/social service; ordained ministry (including women) and active ecumenical engagement.
Church of Sweden.Soteriology: Lutheran emphasis on justification by grace through faith in Christ's atoning death and resurrection; baptism and Eucharist are means of grace; faith is expected to bear fruit in love and service.

Confucianists.Anthropology: Humans are essentially social and improvable through education and ritual. Traditions differ on original nature (Mencius: essentially good; Xunzi: requires disciplined cultivation), but all stress relational roles and self-cultivation.
Confucianists.Cosmology: A harmonious, morally ordered cosmos in which human society mirrors cosmic order; later thought incorporates yin-yang and Five Phases ideas, but emphasis remains on balance and fitting human conduct to Heaven's pattern.
Confucianists.Ecclesiology: Decentralized and non-clerical: no single institutional church or priesthood. Practices are sustained by family, schools, academies, ritual specialists, and historically by state ceremonies honoring Confucius and Heaven.
Confucianists.Epistemology: Knowledge through study, imitation of exemplars, textual tradition, and reflective practice; moral intuition and cultivated disposition matter (with Neo-Confucians debating the role of innate knowledge versus learning).
Confucianists.Eschatology: Little systematic teaching about an afterlife; emphasis is on ancestral veneration, maintaining continuity and reputation, and achieving harmony in this life. Beliefs about spirits/afterlife are often syncretic.
Confucianists.Ethics & Morality: Role-centered, duty-based ethics emphasizing ren (humaneness), li (propriety/ritual), yi (righteousness), zhi (wisdom), and xiao (filial piety). Moral judgment is situational, informed by relationships and social responsibilities.
Confucianists.Exclusivity: Generally non-exclusive and syncretic—compatible with Buddhism, Daoism, and folk religions. Confucianism primarily claims ethical and social authority rather than sole access to spiritual truth.
Confucianists.Metaphysics: Practical, moral-oriented rather than speculative; centers on Tian (Heaven) as a moral order and on principles like li (ritual/principle) and humaneness. Classical Confucius is metaphysically restrained; Neo-Confucians (e.g., Zhu Xi, Wang Yangming) developed more systematic ontologies.
Confucianists.Praxis: Study of the classics, performance of rites, filial and civic duties, moral self-examination, and public service; ritualized behavior and education are the primary means of producing virtue.
Confucianists.Soteriology: No salvation in the supernatural sense; the goal is becoming a junzi/sage and realizing social and moral harmony through self-cultivation, ritual, and ethical conduct—success evaluated this-worldly.

Cypriot Orthodox Church.Anthropology: Humans are body-soul persons made in the image of God, fallen by sin but called to restoration and communion with God (theosis).
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Cosmology: Created ordered universe sustained by God, populated by visible and invisible beings (angels/demons); material creation is good and a vehicle for divine encounter.
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Ecclesiology: An apostolic, conciliar, sacramental Church; the Church of Cyprus is an autocephalous Orthodox Church headed by its Archbishop, with bishops, priests and deacons in apostolic succession.
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Epistemology: Knowledge of God via revelation: Scripture and Holy Tradition (Church Fathers, liturgy, conciliar teaching); emphasis on prayerful and apophatic knowledge rather than abstract proof.
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Eschatology: Belief in Christ’s second coming, bodily resurrection, final judgment and eternal life or separation from God; emphasis on participation in the Kingdom now and to come.
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Ethics & Morality: Moral life centers on repentance, love, the virtues, obedience to Christ and the commandments, supported by ascetic disciplines and communal witness.
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Exclusivity: Holds Orthodoxy as the fullness of apostolic faith while trusting God’s mercy beyond visible boundaries; sacraments and canonical membership remain normative for full participation.
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Metaphysics: Affirms a Trinitarian Christian metaphysics: one God in three persons; reality created by and dependent on God, who is personal, transcendent and immanent.
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Praxis: Liturgical and sacramental life (Divine Liturgy, baptism, chrismation, Eucharist, confession, marriage, etc.), prayer, fasting, veneration of icons, and pastoral/monastic practice.
Cypriot Orthodox Church.Soteriology: Salvation as healing and deification (theosis) through Christ’s incarnation, death and resurrection, mediated by grace in the Church’s life and sacraments.

Druze.Anthropology: Humans are incarnated souls (rūḥ) temporarily bound to bodies, capable of moral and intellectual development; the inner, essential self is the locus of spiritual progress.
Druze.Cosmology: Emanationist: the cosmos unfolds from the One into successive immaterial levels (intellect, soul) down to the material world; history and reality are ordered by these metaphysical gradations and occasional divine epiphanies.
Druze.Ecclesiology: No conventional clergy; religious authority rests with an initiated elite (uqqal) and local councils/elders. The community functions as both a religious and social corpus with internal governance rather than a sacramental church structure.
Druze.Epistemology: Privileges esoteric interpretation (ta'wil) and revealed wisdom preserved in secret epistles, balanced with rational inquiry; authoritative knowledge is transmitted orally and textually by initiated elders and is withheld from the uninitiated.
Druze.Eschatology: Rejects a literal, one‑time bodily resurrection; instead souls undergo successive reincarnations (tanāsukh) until spiritual purification and reunification with the divine. History is viewed in cyclical and spiritual terms rather than a single apocalyptic terminus.
Druze.Ethics & Morality: Emphasizes honesty, loyalty, communal solidarity, modest living, and personal responsibility. Moral life is expressed through ethical behavior, service to the community, and fidelity to inner teachings.
Druze.Exclusivity: Highly exclusive and endogamous: conversion is generally prohibited, religious teachings are secret and reserved for initiates, and community boundaries are strongly policed socially and religiously.
Druze.Metaphysics: Radical monotheism: God is an absolute, transcendent One. Druze thought is heavily Neoplatonic/Isma'ili in influence, positing emanations such as a Universal Intellect and Universal Soul; historically certain figures (most famously al‑Hakim) were understood as divine manifestations in specific formulations.
Druze.Praxis: Religious life is chiefly esoteric and communal rather than ritualistic: study of the secret Rasa'il al‑Hikma, gatherings in khalwa/majlis, guidance by the initiated (uqqal), strict endogamy and strong communal welfare practices; little public ritual, no proselytizing or observance of mainstream Islamic rituals as norms.
Druze.Soteriology: Salvation is achieved by gnosis (esoteric knowledge), ethical conduct, and spiritual purification—processes that typically unfold across successive reincarnations; initiation into the inner circle (uqqal) grants access to full salvific teaching.

Dutch Reformed Church.Anthropology: Humans made in the image of God (Imago Dei) but corrupted by original sin (classically taught as total depravity); persons are moral agents dependent on divine grace for restoration.
Dutch Reformed Church.Cosmology: Creation ex nihilo by God; the world is ordered, good by design but fallen through sin, and unfolds under God's providence and covenantal governance.
Dutch Reformed Church.Ecclesiology: Covenantal and typically presbyterial-synodal in polity (consistory/classis/synod); the visible church comprises believers and their covenant children, with ordained ministry, discipline and sacramental life central.
Dutch Reformed Church.Epistemology: Sola Scriptura: Scripture is the primary norm, interpreted in the light of historic Reformed confessions (Heidelberg Catechism, Belgic Confession, Canons of Dort); reason and tradition serve a subordinate, critical role.
Dutch Reformed Church.Eschatology: Varies by community but classically Reformed tends toward amillennial or non-literal millennial positions, emphasizing Christ’s return, final judgment, resurrection and the consummation of God’s kingdom.
Dutch Reformed Church.Ethics & Morality: Covenantal, Scripture-grounded ethics: obedience to God's law, faithfulness in family and community, stewardship, justice and public responsibility shaped by biblical norms and confessions.
Dutch Reformed Church.Exclusivity: Affirms the necessity of Christ for salvation (salvation in Christ alone) and upholds doctrinal boundaries for the church’s teaching, while maintaining an active commitment to mission and evangelism.
Dutch Reformed Church.Metaphysics: Monotheistic Trinitarian theism: one sovereign, transcendent yet active God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) who is ultimate reality, creator and sustainer of all.
Dutch Reformed Church.Praxis: Corporate worship centered on preaching, Scripture, prayer and the two sacraments (baptism and Lord’s Supper); strong emphasis on catechesis, family piety, church discipline and ordered liturgy.
Dutch Reformed Church.Soteriology: Salvation is by God’s grace alone through faith in Christ alone; historically articulated within Reformed doctrines (e.g., election, effectual calling, perseverance), with some variety over the extent of atonement.

Eastern Orthodox.Anthropology: Humans are embodied image-bearers of God (body–soul unity), fallen by disobedience and illness rather than total corruption, called to healing and restoration through the restoration of the divine likeness (theosis).
Eastern Orthodox.Cosmology: Creation is good and purposeful, sustained by God and intended as a theater of divine-human communion; the material world is sacred and capable of bearing divine grace but is wounded by corruption and enthralled to death until restored.
Eastern Orthodox.Ecclesiology: The Church is the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Body of Christ, structured episcopally with apostolic succession and conciliar (synodal) governance; the Church is both the context and instrument of salvation and sacramental life.
Eastern Orthodox.Epistemology: Knowledge of God is primarily experiential and apophatic (via negativa), mediated by Holy Tradition (Scripture, Fathers, liturgy, icons) and verified by spiritual experience and the life of the Church rather than by purely abstract rational proofs.
Eastern Orthodox.Eschatology: Hope in the resurrection of the body and the new creation; the Kingdom is both present in sacramental life and consummated at Christ’s final manifestation and judgment, culminating in fullness of deification and restored cosmos.
Eastern Orthodox.Ethics & Morality: Ethics is virtue-centered and ascetical, aimed at imitation of Christ and restoration of right relationship with God and others; moral life is enacted liturgically and sacramentally, shaped by prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and cultivation of the virtues.
Eastern Orthodox.Exclusivity: Claims to be the true and fullness-bearing Church of apostolic Christianity, while pastoral theology often allows for God’s merciful action beyond visible boundaries (oikonomia); official stance emphasizes fullness of means of salvation within the Orthodox Church.
Eastern Orthodox.Metaphysics: Relational personalism centered on the triune God; reality is participatory (ontology of persons) and distinguished by the essence–energies distinction (God’s unknowable essence vs. communicable energies) that grounds sacramental participation in divine life.
Eastern Orthodox.Praxis: Communal liturgical worship ( Divine Liturgy ), sacraments (Mysteries) especially Baptism and Eucharist, icon veneration, regular prayer (including the Jesus Prayer), fasting, and monasticism as the privileged school of spiritual formation.
Eastern Orthodox.Soteriology: Salvation is primarily theosis—participation in God’s life effected by Christ’s incarnation, death, and resurrection, realized through baptism, Eucharist, repentance, ascetic struggle, and synergistic cooperation between divine grace and human response.

Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Anthropology: Humans are made in the image of God (Imago Dei), fallen by sin but capable of restoration and deification through Christ and the Church; body and soul are integrally valued in spiritual life.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Cosmology: A created cosmos brought into being by God, comprising visible and invisible realms; angels and demons are active agents, and creation is ordered toward liturgical life and redemption.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Ecclesiology: A hierarchical, apostolic church with bishops, priests and monastic orders, an autocephalous patriarchal structure (since 1959) within the Oriental Orthodox family; the Church is the primary locus of salvation and communal identity.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Epistemology: Authority rests on Scripture and Holy Tradition (including a broader Ethiopian canon), patristic exegesis, liturgy and sacramental/ascetic experience; theological knowledge is both doctrinal and experiential.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Eschatology: Affirms Christ's Second Coming, bodily resurrection, final judgment and eternal communion or separation; emphasis on repentance, prayer and intercession of saints in preparation for the last things.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Ethics & Morality: Moral teaching flows from Scripture, patristic tradition and liturgy, emphasizing virtues, love of neighbor, justice, fasting, chastity, and communal responsibility shaped by monastic and parish life.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Exclusivity: Claims continuity with the original apostolic faith and preserves distinctive rites and canon; sacramental life is centered on the Church—practically particular and protective of its traditions, while recognizing fellow Oriental Orthodox churches and differing from Chalcedonian and Western communions.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Metaphysics: Classical Christian theism: one triune God; Tewahedo (miaphysite) Christology affirms Christ as one united divine-human reality; ultimate grounding of being is God's uncreated reality, with angels and created order participating in that reality.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Praxis: Highly liturgical and sacramental practice: Divine Liturgy (Qeddase) in Ge'ez, veneration of icons and saints, seven (and additional) sacramental rites, strict fasts, monasticism, processions, Tabot/Ark reverence and pilgrimages (e.g., Lalibela, Aksum traditions).
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.Soteriology: Salvation is participation in the incarnation and paschal mystery: grace received through faith, repentance, sacraments, ascetic practice and communal cooperation (synergy) heals sin and leads to union with God.

Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Anthropology: Humans are understood primarily as members of kinship networks and ecological communities; identity and personhood are defined by relationships with family, clan, land, and spirits.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Cosmology: Local creation myths and layered worlds (human, spirit, ancestor) tied to sacred geography; the cosmos is woven with spirits inhabiting natural features and landmarks.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Ecclesiology: Religious authority tends to be decentralized and embedded in kinship groups, temples, or ritual specialists rather than a universal institutional church; leadership is often situational and hereditary or charismatic.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Epistemology: Knowledge is transmitted orally and experientially through stories, rites, elders, shamans, and observation of signs; legitimacy rests on tradition, lineage, and practical efficacy.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Eschatology: Often cyclical or continuity-oriented—emphasis on renewal, ancestral realms, and seasonal regeneration; explicit doctrines of final judgment or cosmic end are uncommon or locally specific.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms derive from tradition, custom, and reciprocal obligations to kin, community, and supernatural beings; ethics emphasize duty, ritual correctness, and practical harmony over abstract moral law.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Exclusivity: Religious identity is frequently bound to ethnicity, place, or lineage; these traditions are not typically missionizing—membership can be fluid but conversion or full participation may require integration into social and ritual networks.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Metaphysics: Divine or spiritual reality is often immanent in nature, ancestors, and local deities; ultimate reality is plural, relational, and grounded in place rather than in abstract universal principles.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Praxis: Rituals, offerings, festivals, rites of passage, divination, and local healing or shamanic practices are central, varying by locality and season and aimed at sustaining relationships with spirits and ancestors.
Ethnic religions—excluding some in separ.Soteriology: Focus is on maintaining harmony, balance, and continuity for the community and ancestors rather than individual salvation; remedies are ritual, social, and restorative rather than doctrinal deliverance.

Evangelical.Anthropology: Humans are created in God's image but marred by original and personal sin, morally responsible beings in need of divine grace and restoration.
Evangelical.Cosmology: God as Creator and Sustainer of an ordered universe; creation is good but fallen through human sin; history is purposeful under divine providence toward redemption.
Evangelical.Ecclesiology: Church seen as a voluntary community of converted believers; local congregations (often autonomous) emphasize preaching, discipleship, missionary outreach, and pastoral leadership.
Evangelical.Epistemology: Primacy of Scripture (often sola scriptura or high biblical authority) interpreted by the Holy Spirit and confirmed by personal conversion and communal testimony; reason and experience have supporting roles.
Evangelical.Eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return, final judgment, resurrection, and eternal destinies; specific timelines vary (premillennialism common but not universal).
Evangelical.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms grounded in the Bible and God's character; emphasis on personal holiness, obedience, and evangelistic/social responsibility, with variation on specific social issues.
Evangelical.Exclusivity: Generally exclusivist: personal faith in Jesus Christ is presented as the essential and normative means of salvation, though some evangelicals allow nuance in how God’s justice may operate.
Evangelical.Metaphysics: Personal, transcendent monotheism: one sovereign God who is both immanent and transcendent; reality includes a supernatural realm (God, angels, demons) alongside the material world.
Evangelical.Praxis: Lived faith centered on Bible reading, prayer, preaching, evangelism/mission, personal testimony, and community practices (often believer's baptism and Lord's Supper as ordinances); active congregational life.
Evangelical.Soteriology: Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ—his atoning death and resurrection effect justification, regeneration, and reconciliation with God; conversion and new birth are central.

Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Anthropology: Humans are created in the image of God with reason and vocation but are corrupted by original and personal sin, unable to attain righteousness apart from God’s forgiving grace.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Cosmology: The material world is God’s good creation, sustained and governed by divine providence; creation is fallen and awaits renewal but is not inherently evil or merely illusory.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Ecclesiology: The Church is the congregation where the Gospel is rightly proclaimed and the sacraments rightly administered; maintains ordained ministry and confessional identity while distinguishing visible and invisible aspects of the Church.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Epistemology: Scripture is the normative authority (sola scriptura), interpreted in the light of the Lutheran confessions (e.g., the Augsburg Confession); reason and tradition have supportive roles but are subordinate to Scripture and faith in God’s promises.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Eschatology: Affirms Christ’s bodily return, the resurrection of the dead, final judgment, and eternal life; emphasis on the sure hope of Christ’s coming rather than elaborate end-times speculation.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Ethics & Morality: Moral life is a grateful response to the Gospel: obedience to God’s commandments, love of neighbor, and faithful fulfillment of vocation; the Law guides and convicts but does not earn salvation.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Exclusivity: Confesses Christ as the unique Savior and that salvation is by grace through faith in him; emphasizes mission and proclamation to all while acknowledging that final judgment and the scope of God’s mercy belong to God alone.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Metaphysics: Affirms a personal Triune God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) as ultimate reality; creation is distinct from the Creator, and both divine transcendence and immanence are affirmed; sin and grace are real, central categories.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Praxis: Corporate liturgical worship centered on Word and Sacrament (preaching, Baptism, Eucharist), regular hymnody and prayer, ordained ministry, catechesis, and diaconal care and service in the world.
Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confe.Soteriology: Justification by grace through faith in Christ alone (sola fide, sola gratia): Christ’s life, death, and resurrection reconcile sinners to God; Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are means of grace that convey forgiveness and strengthen faith.

Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Anthropology: Humans are created in God's image (dignified and relational) but wounded by original sin, inclined to sin and reliant on divine grace for restoration.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Cosmology: Universe created by God out of nothing, ordered and good but now affected by sin and decay; history is providentially governed toward God's redemptive purposes in Christ.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Ecclesiology: The church is the assembly of believers gathered around Word and Sacrament; ordained ministry serves the congregation, the priesthood of all believers is emphasized, and synodical structures govern cooperation among congregations.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Epistemology: Scripture (sola scriptura) is the ultimate norm for faith and doctrine, interpreted in the light of the Lutheran Confessions; reason and tradition are respected but subordinate to the Bible and the witness of the Spirit.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Eschatology: Affirms Christ's bodily return, the resurrection of the dead, final judgment, and eternal life or condemnation; looks forward to the consummation of God's kingdom rather than speculative timetables.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Ethics & Morality: Moral life is shaped by the Law and the Gospel: the Ten Commandments and Christ's teaching guide conduct, while good works flow from faith and vocation rather than earning salvation.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Exclusivity: Confesses Christ as the only Savior (solus Christus) and that justification comes only through faith in Him, while acknowledging that final judgment and the outworking of God's mercy are committed to God alone.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Metaphysics: Affirms a triune, personal God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) as ultimate reality and Creator; the world and persons are created good but contingent upon God's sustaining will.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Praxis: Public worship shaped by Word and Sacrament (regular preaching, Baptism, and Lord's Supper with affirmed real presence), catechesis, pastoral ministry, congregational life and evangelism; social and diaconal service as expression of faith.
Evangelical Lutheran Church of Brazil.Soteriology: Justification by grace through faith alone in Jesus Christ; salvation is the work of God — Christ's atoning death and resurrection are central, received as a gift by faith.

Evangelicalism.Anthropology: Humans are created in God's image but are fallen and sinful, morally accountable, in need of redemption; persons can respond to God though views on free will vary.
Evangelicalism.Cosmology: The universe is created and sustained by God with purposeful design; human sin has marred creation and God providentially governs history (specific views on origins vary).
Evangelicalism.Ecclesiology: Emphasis on the local church as the primary body of believers with pastoral leadership and the priesthood of all believers; governance ranges from congregational to denominational structures and prioritizes mission and discipleship.
Evangelicalism.Epistemology: Primary epistemic authority is the Bible (sola scriptura influence), interpreted through the Holy Spirit and informed by tradition, reason, and experience; personal conversion experience and scriptural study are highly prized.
Evangelicalism.Eschatology: Expectation of Christ's second coming, final judgment, resurrection, and eternal destiny of heaven or hell; specific timelines and models (e.g., premillennialism, amillennialism) vary, with imminence often stressed.
Evangelicalism.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms are grounded in the Bible, stressing personal holiness, sexual morality, and social responsibilities; emphasis on family, charity, and—depending on tradition—either conservative social positions or broader justice concerns.
Evangelicalism.Exclusivity: Generally affirms that salvation is uniquely through Jesus Christ and promotes active evangelism; some individuals and groups adopt more inclusive or nuanced positions.
Evangelicalism.Metaphysics: Belief in a personal, transcendent God (Triune: Father, Son, Holy Spirit) who is active in the world and whose revelation is primarily biblical; reality includes both physical and spiritual realms and the possibility of miracles.
Evangelicalism.Praxis: Worship centers on preaching, Scripture, prayer, and congregational singing; common practices include evangelism, Bible study, prayer meetings, sacraments as ordinances (baptism and Lord's Supper), and missionary activity; charismatic expressions appear in many communities.
Evangelicalism.Soteriology: Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ's atoning death and resurrection, received by repentance and regeneration by the Holy Spirit; assurance of salvation is often emphasized.

Free Church.Anthropology: Humans are created in God’s image yet fallen and morally affected by sin; persons possess conscience and responsibility, with theological emphasis (varies) on human depravity and/or moral freedom.
Free Church.Cosmology: Creation ex nihilo by God; the universe is ordered and sustained by divine providence but fallen and subject to corruption until redemption and renewal.
Free Church.Ecclesiology: Churches independent of state control, typically voluntary membership with either congregational or presbyterian governance; the priesthood of all believers, local autonomy, and disciplined community life are stressed.
Free Church.Epistemology: Primacy of Scripture (sola scriptura) as the rule for faith and practice, with reason, tradition, and experience playing subsidiary roles; communal discernment through preaching and teaching is central.
Free Church.Eschatology: Belief in Christ’s bodily return, final judgment, resurrection of the dead, and new creation; views on millennium and chronology vary (amillennial, premillennial, etc.).
Free Church.Ethics & Morality: Morality grounded in Scripture and formed by discipleship: personal holiness, social responsibility, and often conservative sexual and family ethics; active engagement in charity and justice is common.
Free Church.Exclusivity: Affirms the central Christian claim that salvation is in Christ alone while pastoral and doctrinal approaches to inclusivity and the scope of God’s grace differ among Free Church bodies.
Free Church.Metaphysics: Biblical theism: a personal, triune God who is transcendent and immanent; reality includes both material and spiritual orders and allows for miracles and divine action.
Free Church.Praxis: Worship focused on preaching, Scripture reading, prayer, hymnody, and the ordinances (baptism and the Lord’s Supper); strong emphasis on evangelism, mission, pastoral care, and church discipline.
Free Church.Soteriology: Centered on Christ’s atoning work and justification by grace through faith; emphasis on personal conversion and regeneration by the Holy Spirit (specific doctrines—e.g., predestination vs. conditional election—vary among Free Churches).

Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Anthropology: Human beings are created in the image and likeness of God, fallen by sin but called to restoration and theosis (participation in the divine life). Personhood is relational and oriented to communion with God and others.
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Cosmology: Created order sustained by God; the material world is good and a means of encounter with the divine. The cosmos is ordered teleologically toward deification and liturgical renewal in Christ.
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Ecclesiology: An Eastern Catholic (sui iuris) Church of the Byzantine rite in full communion with the Bishop of Rome. Retains Eastern hierarchical and synodal structures, liturgical patrimony and theological outlook while acknowledging papal primacy within Catholic communion.
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Epistemology: Knowledge of God comes chiefly via revelation: Scripture and the living Tradition (Fathers, liturgy, councils), interpreted within the Church. Emphasizes both cataphatic (affirmative) and apophatic (negative) ways of knowing; liturgy and ascetic experience are epistemic means.
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Eschatology: Affirms the bodily resurrection, Second Coming of Christ, Final Judgment and eternal life. Eschatological hope is framed as consummation in communion with God and the fullness of theosis.
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Ethics & Morality: Moral life centers on repentance, ascetic practice, cultivation of virtues, love of neighbor and participation in the liturgical life. Ethical teaching is rooted in Scripture, patristic tradition, and the commandments as lived in community.
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Exclusivity: Affirms itself as part of the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church in communion with Rome, while recognizing elements of sanctification and truth in other Christian traditions. Holds that the Church is the ordinary means of salvation but trusts in God's mercy beyond visible boundaries.
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Metaphysics: Classical Christian theism: one Triune God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit); reality oriented toward participation in God's life. Emphasizes sacramental realism and often the Eastern apophatic tradition (unknowability of God's essence, experience of God's energies).
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Praxis: Byzantine liturgical life (Divine Liturgy, the Eucharist), sacramental/mysterial life (baptism, chrismation, Eucharist, confession, etc.), veneration of icons, fasting, prayer, and monastic/communal disciplines constitute primary religious practice.
Greek Byzantine Catholic Church.Soteriology: Salvation is primarily understood as healing and deification: the restoration of human nature in Christ through incarnation, death, resurrection and the gift of the Spirit. It is achieved by grace through faith, sacraments, repentance and human cooperation (synergy).

Hinduism.Anthropology: Humans are embodied selves (atman) bound by karma and samsara; identity involves layers (koshas) of body-mind-ego and social roles (dharma, varna/ashrama) that shape life and rebirth.
Hinduism.Cosmology: Cyclic and multi-leveled: vast kalpas (cycles) of creation, preservation, and dissolution, recurring yugas (ages), many lokas (worlds), and periodic appearances of divine beings and avatars within an ordered cosmos.
Hinduism.Ecclesiology: Non-centralized and plural: no single church or hierarchy; authority is dispersed among sampradayas (sectarian traditions), temples, gurus, monastic orders, and local communities, with diverse institutional forms.
Hinduism.Epistemology: Accepts multiple means of knowledge (pramanas): perception and inference, scriptural testimony (shruti/smrti), analogy, and other valid methods, with emphasis on revelation (Vedas) and experiential realization in many schools.
Hinduism.Eschatology: Non-linear and cyclical: no single final judgment; the universe undergoes repeated dissolution and renewal, while individual souls undergo rebirth until liberation ends the cycle for that soul; avatars and world events recur within cycles.
Hinduism.Ethics & Morality: Centered on dharma (duty, righteousness), karma (moral causation), and virtues such as ahimsa (nonviolence) and satya (truth); ethical prescriptions are often contextual, linked to role, stage of life, and tradition.
Hinduism.Exclusivity: Generally pluralistic and tolerant: many Hindu traditions accept multiple valid paths to the divine and can accommodate other religions, though some sects assert doctrinal exclusivity or superiority.
Hinduism.Metaphysics: Plural and diverse: many schools posit an ultimate reality (Brahman) and a true self (Atman) — ranging from nondual (Advaita) identity of Atman and Brahman to dualist (Dvaita) and qualified-nondual (Vishishtadvaita) accounts; also dualist Samkhya distinguishes purusha (spirit) and prakriti (matter).
Hinduism.Praxis: Varied ritual and spiritual practices: temple worship and puja, yajna (sacrificial rites), mantra and bhajan, yoga and meditation, pilgrimages and festivals, plus guru-disciple transmission and daily household rites.
Hinduism.Soteriology: Freedom (moksha) from samsara attained by diverse paths — knowledge (jnana), devotion (bhakti), selfless action (karma yoga), and disciplined practice (raja/yoga) — with doctrines differing on the nature of liberation.

Hoahaoism.Anthropology: Humans are relational pattern-bearers: embodied nodes of the Hoahao with capacities for awareness, empathy, and co-creation; ignorance (misalignment) is the primary condition to be healed, not inherent depravity.
Hoahaoism.Cosmology: The cosmos is cyclical and fractal: worlds unfold from the Hoahao as nested weavings of light and habit, undergo entropic unbinding, and are re-integrated in periodic renewals; creation is ongoing and participatory.
Hoahaoism.Ecclesiology: Organized as dispersed circles and networks of Tenders and apprentices with minimal hierarchical authority; leadership is functional and accountable, emphasizing local autonomy and inter-circle consultation.
Hoahaoism.Epistemology: Knowledge arises from calibrated inner perception (trained attention), corroborated by communal witnessing and pragmatic outcomes; revelation, embodied experience, and iterative verification are privileged over abstract dogma.
Hoahaoism.Eschatology: No single final apocalypse; eschatology emphasizes cyclical renewal and progressive maturation of worlds — pessimism and optimism coexist as phases — with the possibility of remade orders as communities achieve widespread resonance.
Hoahaoism.Ethics & Morality: Ethics center on reciprocity, minimization of harm, fidelity to context-sensitive compassion, and stewardship of webs of life; moral rules are pragmatic guides to preserve resonance and relational health.
Hoahaoism.Exclusivity: Primarily inclusive and pluralistic: Hoahaoism claims robust truth about resonance and practice but treats other spiritual paths as complementary routes to harmony, permitting syncretism while maintaining distinct communal practices.
Hoahaoism.Metaphysics: A layered panentheism positing a single ground of being called the Hoahao — an immanent, intelligent field that both permeates and transcends phenomena; reality is constituted by patterns of resonance within that field.
Hoahaoism.Praxis: Daily practices include collective breath-songs, attentional meditations, ritual tending of communal gardens and memory-stones, seasonal ceremonies marking cosmic rhythms, and apprenticeship with elder Tenders.
Hoahaoism.Soteriology: Salvation is healing into right-resonance with the Hoahao — restoration of balance and integrity called 'Unbinding' — achieved through ethical attunement, disciplined practice, and communal re-tuning rather than juridical forgiveness.

Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Anthropology: Humans are created by God, morally capable but fallen into sin; persons need divine correction and membership in the true church to be restored to right relationship with God.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Cosmology: God as Creator and sovereign governor of the universe; spiritual beings (angels) exist and the created world operates under divine order and moral law.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Ecclesiology: Highly centralized, hierarchical, restorationist ecclesiology: Iglesia ni Cristo claims to be the one true church established by God, led by an Executive Minister and structured congregationally under centralized governance.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Epistemology: The Bible is authoritative but is interpreted and applied by the church’s central leadership; doctrinal truth is taught and declared by the Executive Minister and church administration as the church’s final arbiter.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Eschatology: Belief in the future return of Christ, resurrection, final judgment, and eternal reward or condemnation; emphasis that ultimate vindication belongs to those in the true church.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Ethics & Morality: Conservative moral teaching emphasizing obedience to God and church authority, family values, sexual morality, discipline, communal responsibility and ethical living according to biblical norms as interpreted by the church.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Exclusivity: Explicitly exclusivist: Iglesia ni Cristo teaches it is the unique, true Church of Christ and that membership in it is necessary for salvation.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Metaphysics: Monotheistic: one supreme God (God the Father). Jesus is regarded as God’s Son and a distinct, subordinate being; the Holy Spirit is understood as God’s active power rather than a second person of a Trinity.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Praxis: Regular corporate worship (Sunday and midweek services), baptism by immersion, prayer meetings, evangelism, church-administered rites (weddings, funerals, memorials), and strict organizational discipline and attendance.
Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ).Soteriology: Salvation is achieved through faith expressed by baptism by immersion, repentance, obedience, participation in the church’s sacraments and life; the church teaches that the true Church of Christ is necessary for salvation.

Islam.Anthropology: Humans are created from clay and endowed with a spirit (ruh) and an innate disposition (fitra) toward God; morally accountable agents capable of good and evil. Classical theology debates free will versus divine decree, but persons bear responsibility for their choices.
Islam.Cosmology: The universe is God-created and purposeful, marked by divine signs (ayat); Islamic texts describe layered heavens and an ordered cosmos governed by God's will, with seen and unseen dimensions pointing to moral and eschatological ends.
Islam.Ecclesiology: The Muslim community (ummah) is the primary social-religious unit; authority is largely decentralized and vested in scholars (ulama), jurists, and local imams. Sunni Islam has no single clergy head; Shia Islam features hierarchies of learned jurists (marjaʿiyya).
Islam.Epistemology: Primary epistemic authority is revelation: the Quran and the Prophet's Sunnah. Juristic methods (ijtihad), consensus (ijma), analogy (qiyas) and human reason (aql) also inform knowledge and law, with sectarian variations in weight and method.
Islam.Eschatology: Belief in bodily resurrection, a Day of Judgment, accountability, reward (jannah) and punishment (jahannam); eschatological signs, prophetic intercession, and the weighing of deeds figure prominently.
Islam.Ethics & Morality: Moral life is grounded in divine law (sharia) derived from the Quran and Sunnah, emphasizing justice, mercy, charity, honesty, and communal obligations; intention (niyyah) and context inform ethical assessment.
Islam.Exclusivity: Islam teaches that Muhammad is the final prophet and the Quran the final revelation, claiming normative truth for its vision of God and salvation. Attitudes toward non-Muslims vary: 'People of the Book' have a special status, and theological views range from exclusivist (only explicit submission ensures salvation) to emphases on God's mercy and ultimate judgment beyond human knowledge.
Islam.Metaphysics: Radical monotheism (tawhid): one transcendent, personal God (Allah) with communicable and incomprehensible attributes; reality includes unseen beings (angels, jinn) and prophets who convey divine revelation. There is no incarnation; creation depends continuously on God.
Islam.Praxis: Core religious practice centers on the Five Pillars: profession of faith (shahada), five daily prayers (salat), almsgiving (zakat), fasting in Ramadan (sawm), and pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj), along with ritual purity, dietary rules, and communal worship (jumʿa).
Islam.Soteriology: Salvation consists in submission to God (Islam) expressed through faith (iman), righteous deeds (amal), repentance, and reliance on God's mercy. There is no original sin; ethical conduct and observance of God's commands, together with divine grace, determine final standing.

Jainism.Anthropology: Humans are embodied jivas (souls) possessing consciousness and moral agency; identity and fate are determined by karmic influx, producing repeated rebirths across life forms until purification.
Jainism.Cosmology: An eternal, cyclical cosmos structured vertically (lower worlds, middle human world, heavens) and temporally (ascending/descending eras); the universe is uncreated and operates by natural law.
Jainism.Ecclesiology: A sangha of monks, nuns, and lay followers with strong monastic leadership (acharyas); organizationally decentralized and divided mainly into Digambara and Svetambara sects with differing scriptural and practical norms.
Jainism.Epistemology: Anekantavada (many-sidedness) and syadvada (conditional predication) emphasize relative perspectives; primary pramanas (means of valid knowledge) include perception, inference, and trustworthy testimony.
Jainism.Eschatology: No permanent heaven or hell: karmic results produce temporary heavenly or hellish rebirths; liberated souls attain Siddhashila and remain eternally free from the cycle of rebirth.
Jainism.Ethics & Morality: Ahimsa (non-violence) is supreme, supported by truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity, and non-attachment; strict vegetarianism, care for all living beings, and varying levels of austerity are central moral commitments.
Jainism.Exclusivity: Salvation is theoretically available to all souls regardless of birth; Jainism generally does not proselytize and stresses individual self-effort—though sectarian histories include debates (e.g., about women's eligibility for liberation).
Jainism.Metaphysics: Dualistic realism: eternal individual souls (jiva) and non-soul reality (ajiva); karma is conceived as subtle material particles that bind to jiva and obscure its innate consciousness; no creator god.
Jainism.Praxis: Monastic renunciation and severe austerities for monks/nuns; lay practices include vows, fasting, ritual repentance (pratikraman), meditation (samayika), and communal rituals; some communities practice sallekhana (ritual fast-to-death).
Jainism.Soteriology: Liberation (moksha) is the complete eradication of karmic matter from the soul, achieved through the Three Jewels—right faith, right knowledge, right conduct—and rigorous ethical discipline and ascetic practice.

Jehovah's Witnesses.Anthropology: Humans are created mortal beings with no inherent immortal soul; death is unconsciousness. Personality and life are a gift from God; hope for individuals rests in resurrection by God’s power.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Cosmology: God created the heavens and the earth; Satan is a created angel who rebelled and now opposes God. The material universe is created and sustained by Jehovah, and current world order is under Satan’s influence until God intervenes.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Ecclesiology: Highly centralized movement governed by a small Governing Body that directs doctrine and policy. Local congregations are led by elders and ministerial servants; membership is organized and monitored through meetings, preaching activity records, and formal rites like baptism.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Epistemology: Primary authority is the Bible (New World Translation) interpreted by the Governing Body. Doctrinal guidance comes from Watch Tower Society publications and congregational teaching; claimed reliance on Holy Spirit guidance as mediated through the organization.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Eschatology: Apocalyptic expectation of imminent end to the current system at Armageddon, followed by Christ’s millennial reign. Teaches that Jesus began ruling invisibly in 1914; a limited heavenly class (144,000) will reign with Christ, while a greater number have the prospect of earthly eternal life through resurrection.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Ethics & Morality: Moral life is guided by a literal, conservative reading of the Bible: sexual chastity, honesty, family responsibilities, neutrality in politics and warfare, and prohibition of blood transfusions. Celebrations and practices seen as pagan or nationalistic (e.g., most holidays, saluting flags) are avoided.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Exclusivity: Claims to be the sole true Christian organization and God’s approved channel in the last days. Other religions are viewed as false or under Satanic influence; association and salvation outside the organization are seen as jeopardized.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Metaphysics: Monotheistic, using the name Jehovah for God. Rejects the Trinity: God (Jehovah) is the one supreme Person, Jesus is his first created Son (identified with Michael the archangel), and the Holy Spirit is God’s impersonal active force.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Praxis: Emphasis on regular door‑to‑door evangelism, congregation meetings at Kingdom Halls, Bible study, annual Memorial of Christ’s death, and baptism by full immersion. Congregational discipline includes disfellowshipping and avoidance (shunning) of unrepentant former members.
Jehovah's Witnesses.Soteriology: Salvation depends on faith in Jesus’ ransom sacrifice plus obedience to Jehovah as interpreted by the organization: preaching, baptism, moral conduct, and loyalty to God’s kingdom. Resurrection and everlasting life are granted according to God’s judgment; salvation is conditional rather than automatic.

Judaism.Anthropology: Humans are created b'tselem Elohim (in the image of God), endowed with moral agency and free will; moral/psychic inclinations (yetzer tov and yetzer ra) require ethical discipline and observance of commandments.
Judaism.Cosmology: God created and sustains the universe (Genesis traditions); history is linear and providentially guided toward redemption, with natural law governing creation and room for divine intervention and miracles.
Judaism.Ecclesiology: Non‑hierarchical and community‑centered rather than church‑centered; organized around synagogues, rabbis and communal institutions, with multiple denominations (Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist, etc.).
Judaism.Epistemology: Primary knowledge comes from revelation (Torah) and prophetic tradition interpreted through rabbinic discourse; reason, legal precedent, debate, and lived practice inform truth and authority.
Judaism.Eschatology: Diverse expectations: a messianic age, ingathering of exiles, resurrection of the dead and a perfected world (Olam Ha‑Ba); understandings range from literal messiah and bodily resurrection to symbolic or ethical visions of future redemption.
Judaism.Ethics & Morality: Rooted in Torah and rabbinic law (halakha) combining ritual and interpersonal commandments, emphasizing justice (tzedek), charity (tzedakah), and tikkun olam (repairing the world).
Judaism.Exclusivity: Affirms a particular covenantal election of the Jewish people with distinct obligations, but generally recognizes righteous non‑Jews (Noahide ethics) and does not uniformly claim exclusive access to moral or salvific truth; interpretations of chosenness and universalism vary across movements.
Judaism.Metaphysics: Monotheistic: a single, indivisible God (YHWH) who is transcendent yet immanent, the creator and moral governor; divine attributes are often expressed negatively (what God is not), and God enters a covenantal relationship with Israel.
