Judaism.Praxis: Daily and seasonal practices: prayer, Sabbath observance, festivals, kashrut, life‑cycle rites, and Torah study; communal worship in synagogues and halakhic observance shape Jewish life.
Judaism.Soteriology: Focuses on teshuvah (repentance), observance of mitzvot, prayer and righteous deeds as means of moral restoration and communal redemption; beliefs about individual afterlife reward vary across streams (Olam Ha‑Ba, Gan Eden, Gehenna, resurrection).

Maronite Church.Anthropology: Humans made in the image of God (body–soul unity), fallen by sin but capable of restoration; vocation is communion with God through prayer, sacraments, and community life.
Maronite Church.Cosmology: Created, ordered cosmos with spiritual beings (angels, demons); God transcendent yet immanent by providence and presence in the sacraments and liturgy; liturgical life sanctifies creation.
Maronite Church.Ecclesiology: A sui iuris Eastern Catholic Church in full communion with Rome, led by the Patriarch of Antioch and synods of bishops; apostolic succession, hierarchical clergy, balance of eastern tradition and catholic unity.
Maronite Church.Epistemology: Knowledge through Scripture and Holy Tradition interpreted by the Church Fathers and Magisterium; liturgy as theological expression; reason illumined by faith.
Maronite Church.Eschatology: Belief in Christ’s second coming, resurrection of the body, final judgment, and eternal destinies (heaven, hell; acceptance of purgatorial purification in Catholic doctrine); emphasis on hope and theosis/participation in divine life.
Maronite Church.Ethics & Morality: Moral teaching grounded in Scripture, the Beatitudes and Ten Commandments, patristic tradition and Catholic social teaching; emphasizes charity, family, chastity, and the Christian virtues.
Maronite Church.Exclusivity: Affirms the Church as the ordinary means of salvation and the fullness of Christian truth in communion with Rome, while recognizing elements of truth and sanctification outside its visible boundaries in line with Catholic teaching.
Maronite Church.Metaphysics: Classical Christian metaphysics: one triune God (Father, Son, Spirit); Jesus Christ fully God and fully human; created reality sustained by God; sacraments as real means of divine grace.
Maronite Church.Praxis: Liturgical and sacramental life (Antiochene/West Syriac tradition, Divine Liturgy of St. James), regular Eucharist, fasting, feasts, prayer, veneration of Mary and the saints, strong parish and monastic presence.
Maronite Church.Soteriology: Salvation through Christ’s incarnation, death, and resurrection; divine grace conferred especially in the sacraments; cooperation of faith and works, with Marian and patristic devotions shaping understanding.

Methodist.Anthropology: Humans are created in the imago Dei but fallen; persons possess moral agency and free will (Wesleyan-Arminian emphasis), capable of responding to or resisting God’s grace.
Methodist.Cosmology: The universe is God’s creation (ex nihilo), ordered and good but marred by the Fall; God remains immanent and transcendent, upholding and redeeming creation toward restoration.
Methodist.Ecclesiology: Connectional church structure balancing local congregations and wider denominational oversight (often with bishops and itinerant ministry); sacraments administered publicly, active lay participation, and organized mission networks.
Methodist.Epistemology: Scripture is primary for doctrine, interpreted through the Wesleyan Quadrilateral—Scripture, tradition, reason, and experience—with attention to personal conversion and experiential assurance of faith.
Methodist.Eschatology: Affirms Christ’s return, resurrection, final judgment, and eternal reward or separation; emphasis is pastoral and ethical—living in hopeful expectancy and holiness—rather than speculative end-time systems.
Methodist.Ethics & Morality: Moral life centers on love of God and neighbor with emphases on personal holiness and social holiness—works of piety and mercy, justice, temperance, and care for the poor guided by Scripture, reason, tradition, and experience.
Methodist.Exclusivity: Christ-centered and evangelical: Jesus Christ is the decisive Savior; salvation is offered to all through Christ via prevenient grace, while ultimate access is held to come through Christ, with openness about God’s mercy in particular cases.
Methodist.Metaphysics: Classical Christian theism: one personal God in Trinity (Father, Son, Spirit); creation is real and good, the world sustained by God's providence, and spiritual realities (sin, grace, angels) are real and efficacious.
Methodist.Praxis: Worship with preaching, hymnody, sacraments (Baptism and Eucharist as means of grace), prayer, Bible study, small groups (class meetings), mission and social action; ordained and lay ministries engage congregation and community.
Methodist.Soteriology: Salvation is by God’s prevenient grace enabling response, justification by faith, and ongoing sanctification (including the Wesleyan ideal of entire sanctification); grace is universal in offer, not irresistible.

Mormons.Anthropology: Humans are literal spirit children of God endowed with agency and moral accountability, sent to mortal life to learn, be tested, form families, and progress spiritually toward eventual resurrection and potential exaltation.
Mormons.Cosmology: Pre-mortal existence of spirits, creation as organization of eternal matter by divine beings (Jehovah/Elohim), multiple worlds and a purposeful mortal probation on Earth as part of God's plan.
Mormons.Ecclesiology: A centralized, hierarchical restorationist church led by a prophet-president and councils (Quorum of the Twelve, First Presidency) with priesthood offices (Aaronic and Melchizedek), organized into wards and stakes and distinct temple and meetinghouse functions.
Mormons.Epistemology: Knowledge is grounded in scripture (Bible, Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, Pearl of Great Price), continuing revelation through a living prophet and personal confirmation by the Holy Ghost; testimony is valued as spiritual evidence.
Mormons.Eschatology: Anticipates Christ’s Second Coming, a millennial reign, universal resurrection, final judgment, and eternal assignment to three kingdoms of glory (celestial, terrestrial, telestial), with exaltation in the celestial kingdom as the highest outcome.
Mormons.Ethics & Morality: Emphasis on family, chastity, honesty, service, compassion, obedience to commandments, and health/temporal codes (e.g., Word of Wisdom); moral life is oriented toward covenantal fidelity and community welfare.
Mormons.Exclusivity: Claims to be the restored original church with exclusive priesthood authority to perform saving ordinances necessary for highest exaltation, while practicing vicarious ordinances for the dead and emphasizing missionary outreach and God’s mercy for others.
Mormons.Metaphysics: Godhead comprises God the Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost as distinct personages; God has an embodied, exalted existence and human beings are eternal spirit children of heavenly parents with the potential to progress toward godhood (exaltation).
Mormons.Praxis: Regular worship includes weekly sacrament, lay-led congregations, missionary work, tithing and offerings, temple ordinances (including proxy work for the dead), family-centered practices (family prayer and home evening), and service.
Mormons.Soteriology: Salvation centers on Jesus Christ's atonement; it requires faith, repentance, baptism by proper priesthood authority, receipt of the Holy Ghost, obedience to covenants and ordinances (including temple rites), with grace enabling redemption and works evidencing faith; final reward includes degrees of glory.

Netherlands Reformed Churches.Anthropology: Humans made in God's image but corrupted by the Fall; total depravity in tendency and will, moral responsibility, and need for divine regeneration.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Cosmology: Creation ex nihilo; the universe exists for God's glory and is governed providentially by God, fallen along with humanity but sustained until Christ's consummation.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Ecclesiology: Confessional, covenantal church life with Presbyterian‑synodal governance (elders, deacons, classes/synods); the visible church is the covenant community administering Word and sacraments.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Epistemology: Sola Scriptura: the Bible is the ultimate authority, interpreted within the framework of historic Reformed confessions (Belgic Confession, Heidelberg Catechism, Canons of Dort); reason and tradition are subordinate aids.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Eschatology: Generally amillennial or non‑dispensational: Christ's bodily return, final resurrection and judgment, and the full consummation of God's kingdom—emphasis on assurance and final restoration rather than detailed timeline speculation.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Ethics & Morality: Covenant-based moral order grounded in Scripture and the Ten Commandments; emphasis on holiness, family responsibility, conservative sexual ethics, and faithful neighbor-love/social duty.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Exclusivity: Affirms the uniqueness of Christ as the only Savior; offers membership and sacramental participation to baptized believers and their covenant children while expecting doctrinal conformity; other Christian bodies may be respected but are judged by doctrinal fidelity.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Metaphysics: Trinitarian theism: one sovereign, personal God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit); supernatural reality, creation sustained by God, sin and grace real powers in human life.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Praxis: Worship centered on preaching and Scripture, regular sacraments (infant baptism and the Lord's Supper), catechism instruction, psalm/hymn singing, prayer, and church discipline; simple, confessional liturgy.
Netherlands Reformed Churches.Soteriology: Classic Reformed/Calvinist: salvation by grace through Christ alone, justification by faith, election and effectual calling (particular redemption as formulated in the Canons of Dort), and perseverance of the saints.

Orthodox.Anthropology: Humans are embodied persons made in the image and likeness of God; the image is ineradicable while the likeness is recoverable through healing and theosis, with freedom and responsibility emphasized.
Orthodox.Cosmology: The world is a good, created order intended to glorify God; it is fallen but redeemable, understood sacramentally as the theater of God's restorative actions toward creation.
Orthodox.Ecclesiology: The Church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic, constituted sacramentally and episcopally; organized in autocephalous churches with conciliar (synodal) governance and emphasis on apostolic continuity.
Orthodox.Epistemology: Knowledge of God is primarily experiential and ecclesial—theoria or mystical vision—grounded in Scripture, the Church Fathers, liturgy, and apophatic theology; reason serves tradition and experience.
Orthodox.Eschatology: Focuses on bodily resurrection, final judgment, and the renewal of creation; eschatology is seen as the consummation of theosis and participation in the new creation, often taught with apophatic reserve about specifics.
Orthodox.Ethics & Morality: Ethics emphasizes virtues and the purification of passions, imitation of Christ, love and humility, pursued within communal and liturgical life rather than abstract legalism.
Orthodox.Exclusivity: Claims to preserve the fullness of apostolic faith and sacramental life and thus a unique salvific role, while acknowledging God's mercy and engaging cautiously in ecumenical dialogue; sacramental communion is generally restricted to Orthodox faithful.
Orthodox.Metaphysics: God is transcendent yet personally present; reality is created by God and participation in God's uncreated energies (Palamite distinction of essence and energies) is possible, stressing a relational, sacramental ontology.
Orthodox.Praxis: Centered on liturgy and sacraments (Eucharist, baptism, chrismation), regular prayer (including the Jesus Prayer), fasting, confession, monasticism, and the use of icons as windows to the divine.
Orthodox.Soteriology: Salvation is primarily theosis—healing and divinization in Christ—accomplished through incarnation, sacraments, repentance, prayer, and cooperative (synergistic) human response to divine grace.

Orthodox Church of Greece.Anthropology: Sees humans as body-soul unities made in the image and likeness of God, fallen but not annihilated; the human vocation is healing and restoration (theosis)—growing into likeness to God through grace and ascetic struggle.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Cosmology: Believes God created the world ex nihilo and sustains it by providence; the cosmos is ordered, populated by angels and susceptible to corruption by sin, and is meant to be sanctified through Christ, liturgy and sacramental life.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Ecclesiology: An autocephalous member of the Eastern Orthodox communion with episcopal apostolic succession and conciliar (synodal) governance; the Church is understood as the Body of Christ and the sacramental locus of salvation and truth.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Epistemology: Relies on divine revelation transmitted in Scripture and Holy Tradition, interpreted by the Fathers and ecumenical councils; values both doctrinal teaching and apophatic/mystical knowledge gained in liturgical and ascetic experience.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Eschatology: Affirms Christ's second coming, the general resurrection, final judgment and the fulfillment of God's kingdom; stresses present participation in eternal life through the Church while awaiting consummation.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Ethics & Morality: Grounded in the commandments and the imitation of Christ, emphasizing virtues (love, humility, mercy), ascetic disciplines, communal responsibility and moral transformation rather than legalistic rule-following.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Exclusivity: Claims to preserve the apostolic and patristic faith as fullness of Christian truth; while recognizing elements of truth and sanctity in other Christians, it regards full sacramental and ecclesial communion as belonging to Orthodox Church and typically requires Orthodox reception for full participation.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Metaphysics: Affirms one Triune God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) who is transcendent yet personally present; distinguishes God's unknowable essence from knowable energies (Palamite theology) and holds a sacramental realism in which created reality can partake in divine life.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Praxis: Centered on the Divine Liturgy and the seven major sacraments (baptism, chrismation, Eucharist, confession, marriage, ordination, unction), plus fasting, daily prayer, veneration of icons and a strong monastic tradition as vehicles of spiritual formation.
Orthodox Church of Greece.Soteriology: Salvation is primarily theosis—participation in divine life accomplished by Christ's incarnation, death and resurrection and effected through synergistic cooperation between divine grace and human repentance, faith, sacraments and works.

Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Anthropology: Humans are body-and-soul persons made in God’s image; the Fall wounded but did not annihilate that image. The human vocation is restoration and transformation (theosis) into communion with God through repentance, prayer, and virtue.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Cosmology: The world is God’s good creation, inhabited by visible and invisible beings (angels/demons). Creation is fallen but remains capable of being healed and transfigured, with an emphasis on the sacramental and sacramentalized material order.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Ecclesiology: The Church is apostolic, Eucharistic, and hierarchical (bishops, priests, deacons) governed synodally. The Orthodox Church of Ukraine presents itself as an autocephalous local Orthodox Church for Ukraine (granted by Constantinople in 2019) and claims continuity with Eastern Orthodox tradition, though its status is disputed by some other Orthodox bodies.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Epistemology: Knowledge of God comes through Holy Scripture, Holy Tradition (including the Church Fathers and ecumenical councils), liturgy and prayer, and mystical experience; reason and experience are integrated but interpreted within the living tradition of the Church.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Eschatology: Affirms Christ’s Second Coming, the resurrection of the dead, final judgment, and the eternal destinies of heaven and hell; stresses an ‘already/not-yet’ kingdom where present liturgical life anticipates and participates in the final consummation and transfiguration of creation.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Ethics & Morality: Moral life follows Christ’s commandments and the virtues taught by Scripture and the Fathers—love, humility, mercy, chastity—expressed in both personal asceticism and communal responsibilities, with strong emphasis on repentance and pastoral discernment.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Exclusivity: Maintains that Orthodox Christianity preserves the fullest sacramental and doctrinal life of the Church, and the OCU asserts canonical jurisdiction in Ukraine; it recognizes other Christian traditions for dialogue and pastoral contact but upholds confessional boundaries and Orthodox ecclesial claims.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Metaphysics: One transcendent, personal God in three Persons (Trinity); Christ as the incarnate Logos. Reality is sacramental: created being participates in divine life while God’s essence remains ultimately unknowable though God’s energies are present to the world.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Praxis: Liturgical and sacramental life is central: the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, icons, seven major sacraments (Baptism, Chrismation, Eucharist, Confession, Matrimony, Ordination, Unction), fasting, the liturgical year, and monasticism shape belief and practice.
Orthodox Church of Ukraine.Soteriology: Salvation is primarily deification (theosis): a lifelong, therapeutic process of healing and union with God effected by Christ, mediated by grace and human cooperation (synergy) in the sacraments, asceticism, prayer, and repentance rather than forensic legal justification alone.

Other Christian.Anthropology: Affirms human dignity as created by God; views on human nature vary from doctrines of original sin and deep fallenness to more optimistic emphases on human goodness and cooperative grace.
Other Christian.Cosmology: Typically holds that God created and sustains the universe and that reality includes both material and spiritual dimensions (e.g., angels, demons, providence), though beliefs about supernatural intervention differ.
Other Christian.Ecclesiology: Conceptions of the church vary from institutional, hierarchical bodies to autonomous congregations and loose networks; roles of clergy, sacraments, and lay participation differ across groups.
Other Christian.Epistemology: Sources of knowledge include Scripture, tradition, reason, and experience in different balances; some communities prioritize sola scriptura while others give greater weight to tradition, liturgy, or perceived ongoing revelation.
Other Christian.Eschatology: Wide spectrum of end‑times beliefs—premillennial, amillennial, postmillennial, realized eschatology, and views about judgment, heaven, hell, and possible universal restoration all appear in various communities.
Other Christian.Ethics & Morality: Moral guidance derives from Scripture, Jesus' teachings, tradition, reason, and conscience; common emphases include love, justice, repentance, and holiness, with diverse stances on contemporary social issues.
Other Christian.Exclusivity: Positions range from strict exclusivism (explicit faith in Christ as the only means of salvation) to inclusivist or universalist views that allow for salvation or final reconciliation beyond explicit Christian confession.
Other Christian.Metaphysics: Varies widely; generally theistic and often personalist, ranging from classical Trinitarian affirmations of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to non‑Trinitarian or more symbolic understandings of Christ and the divine.
Other Christian.Praxis: Worship and religious practice range from formal liturgy and sacramental observance to charismatic, revivalist, or informal styles; common practices include prayer, Scripture reading, baptism, and communion in varying forms and frequencies.
Other Christian.Soteriology: Centered on Jesus Christ's saving work, understood variously as penal substitution, Christus Victor, moral exemplar, or transformative encounter; means of salvation are debated (faith alone, faith plus works, sacraments, or experiential conversion).

Other syncretists.Anthropology: Views humans as composite beings (body, psyche, spirit, ancestors, social roles) whose identity is formed through relationships with community, spirits, nature, and cultural narratives drawn from diverse sources.
Other syncretists.Cosmology: Hybrid cosmologies that merge creation stories and structural schemes (e.g., layered heavens/underworlds, cycles of rebirth, or a single unfolding cosmos), emphasizing relational links among realms rather than a single canonical account.
Other syncretists.Ecclesiology: Institutional forms range from loose, networked communities and charismatic leaders to syncretic congregations; authority is frequently decentralized and legitimacy derives from ritual effectiveness and lineage rather than strict hierarchy.
Other syncretists.Epistemology: Epistemic pluralism—validates multiple sources of knowledge (scripture, revelation, ritual efficacy, dream/vision, ancestral testimony, reason, empirical healing outcomes), often privileging experiential confirmation.
Other syncretists.Eschatology: Varied and flexible: may include cyclical renewal, personal or communal transformation, limited apocalyptic themes, or pragmatic hopes for restoration; eschatological claims are often symbolic and adaptive.
Other syncretists.Ethics & Morality: Practical, context-sensitive ethics focused on relational duties, harmony, reciprocity, and pragmatic outcomes; moral norms are often negotiated syncretically and can incorporate ritual obligations, social care, and moral teachings from various sources.
Other syncretists.Exclusivity: Tends toward inclusivism or pluralism—embraces borrowing and accommodation while sometimes maintaining boundary markers around identity or proprietary practices; exclusivist claims are less common but can appear in particular groups.
Other syncretists.Metaphysics: Ontologically pluralistic and eclectic—combines ideas of material and spiritual realities, ancestral or spirit beings, and often both immanent and transcendent dimensions drawn from multiple traditions.
Other syncretists.Praxis: Eclectic ritual life: blended liturgies, ceremonies, devotional practices, magic/healing techniques, pilgrimage, and adaptation of symbols and rites from multiple traditions to meet communal and individual needs.
Other syncretists.Soteriology: Salvation or flourishing is usually framed as integration, balance, healing, knowledge, or harmony—attained by combining practices and insights from the blended traditions rather than exclusive doctrinal assent.

Anthropology.Charismatic: Similar view of human sinfulness and need for the Spirit, often stressing ongoing formation and empowerment within communal and denominational life.
Anthropology.Pentecostal: Humans are image-bearers who are fallen and in urgent need of conversion and empowerment by the Spirit for sanctification and mission.

Cosmology.Charismatic: Affirms the same spiritual realm but varies in emphasis and may frame spiritual realities within liturgical, sacramental, or pastoral models.
Cosmology.Pentecostal: A spiritually active cosmos: God, angels, demons, and spirits interact with the material world; heavy emphasis on spiritual warfare and deliverance.

Ecclesiology.Charismatic: A cross-denominational movement that renews existing churches; less institutional separation and more networking, renewal groups, and prophetic leaders within established bodies.
Ecclesiology.Pentecostal: Often congregational or denominational, with strong pastoral leadership, rapid church planting, and distinct Pentecostal institutions and networks.

Epistemology.Charismatic: Balances Scripture, tradition, and institutional teaching with Spirit-led experience; charismatic revelations are valued but often interpreted within existing theological frameworks.
Epistemology.Pentecostal: Scripture is authoritative but experiential knowing via the Holy Spirit (tongues, prophecy, inner witness) is privileged as confirmation and guidance.

Eschatology.Charismatic: Eschatological views vary widely by denominational background—some premillennial, others amillennial or less literal—no single dominant schema.
Eschatology.Pentecostal: Frequently premillennial and imminence-focused (expectation of Christ's soon return), with popular dispensational influences in many communities.

Ethics & Morality.Charismatic: Ethical emphases range widely—from conservative holiness to socially progressive—shaped by the host denomination or cultural context.
Ethics & Morality.Pentecostal: Strong emphasis on personal holiness, moral discipline, and often conservative stances on sexual and social ethics, rooted in experiential piety.

Exclusivity.Charismatic: Also affirms Christian uniqueness of salvation in Christ but tends toward ecumenical openness to the Spirit's work across denominational lines and traditions.
Exclusivity.Pentecostal: Affirms salvation in Christ as exclusive; some strands place normative importance on Spirit baptism or charismatic evidence as marks of true Christian experience.

Metaphysics.Charismatic: Also Christian theism stressing the Holy Spirit's current work, often integrated into diverse theological frameworks and worship traditions.
Metaphysics.Pentecostal: Classical Christian theism with a strong emphasis on the present, personal activity of the Holy Spirit and supernatural gifts as ongoing realities.

Praxis.Charismatic: Similar charismatic practices (tongues, prophecy, healing) but frequently embedded within mainline, Catholic, or liturgical services and renewal movements.
Praxis.Pentecostal: Expressive, spontaneous worship with tongues, prophecy, healing, laying on of hands, altar calls, and renewal-focused meetings; often congregational and mission-oriented.

Soteriology.Charismatic: Affirms salvation by faith; charismatic gifts and Spirit empowerment are seen as part of the normal Christian life but are taught and experienced more variably (less uniformly presented as a distinct second work).
Soteriology.Pentecostal: Salvation by faith in Christ, typically with a further distinctive experience of Spirit baptism (often evidenced by speaking in tongues) as empowerment for Christian living.

Presbyterianism.Anthropology: Humans are made in God's image with dignity, reason, and responsibility; the Fall brought corruption (often described as total or pervasive depravity), so divine grace is required for true renewal.
Presbyterianism.Cosmology: The universe is intentionally created good by God, ordered and sustained by providence; it is fallen through sin yet remains under God's redemptive purposes within covenantal structures.
Presbyterianism.Ecclesiology: Governing by elders (presbyters) in representative assemblies (session, presbytery, synod, General Assembly); the church is a covenant community and primary means of grace for worship, nurture, and discipline.
Presbyterianism.Epistemology: Holds Scripture (sola scriptura) as the primary source of theological truth, interpreted in light of historic confessions (e.g., Westminster), informed by reason and tradition but subordinate to biblical authority.
Presbyterianism.Eschatology: Focuses on Christ's return, final judgment, and the renewal of creation; many Presbyterians adopt amillennial or covenantal frameworks, though eschatological views vary within the tradition.
Presbyterianism.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms derive primarily from Scripture and covenantal law (e.g., Ten Commandments), stressing personal holiness, communal responsibility, social justice, and faithful stewardship of creation.
Presbyterianism.Exclusivity: Affirms Christ as the sole mediator and necessary Savior for salvation and maintains doctrinal boundaries for membership and ordination; pastoral approaches to non-Christians and interfaith engagement differ among congregations.
Presbyterianism.Metaphysics: Affirms a transcendent, sovereign, triune God as ultimate reality and ground of being; the created order is real but dependent on God's continuous providence and will.
Presbyterianism.Praxis: Worship centers on preaching, prayer, Scripture reading, and the two sacraments (baptism and Lord's Supper); congregational life is disciplined and ordered, with ordained elders overseeing congregational care and governance.
Presbyterianism.Soteriology: Salvation is by God's grace alone through faith in Christ alone, grounded in doctrines of election and justification by faith; historic Presbyterianism follows Reformed (Calvinist) emphases on predestination, atonement, and sanctification, with some variation across branches.

Protestant.Anthropology: Humans made in God's image (imago Dei) but fallen and morally compromised; persons are morally responsible, dependent on grace for restoration, and called to vocation and stewardship.
Protestant.Cosmology: Universe created by God (creation ex nihilo), ordered and sustained by divine providence; the created order is good but affected by corruption because of sin.
Protestant.Ecclesiology: Diverse polities (congregational, presbyterian, episcopal) but generally affirms local congregational centrality and the priesthood of all believers; denominational and parachurch structures are common.
Protestant.Epistemology: Holds Scripture as the ultimate norm for faith and life; reason, tradition, and experience are consulted but subordinate to the Bible; endorses the 'priesthood of all believers' in interpretation, producing interpretive plurality.
Protestant.Eschatology: Belief in Christ's return, final judgment, resurrection of the dead, and new creation is normative; specific timelines and models (premillennial, amillennial, postmillennial) vary widely among Protestants.
Protestant.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms rooted chiefly in Scripture (sola scriptura) and shaped by conscience and discipleship; stresses personal holiness, social responsibility, and diverse applications across contexts and traditions.
Protestant.Exclusivity: Generally Christocentric—salvation is through Christ—though views range from strict exclusivism to inclusivism and pluralistic tendencies in some liberal strands; most traditions maintain some form of particularity about Christ's role in salvation.
Protestant.Metaphysics: Affirms classical theism: one personal, triune God who is transcendent and immanent, creator and sustainer of all things; reality is ultimately grounded in God's being, though emphases on divine sovereignty and human freedom vary.
Protestant.Praxis: Worship emphasizes preaching and Scripture; common observance of two ordinances/sacraments (baptism, Lord's Supper) with varying understandings; strong emphasis on evangelism, mission, and congregational participation.
Protestant.Soteriology: Centered on salvation through Christ by grace through faith (sola gratia, sola fide) with Christ's atoning work decisive; debates persist (e.g., Calvinist vs. Arminian) about election, assurance, and perseverance.

Protestant Churches without free churche.Anthropology: Humans are made in the image of God, possessing dignity and relational/social vocation; by sin the image is marred but not obliterated, so persons retain reason, conscience and capacity for moral choice and relationship with God.
Protestant Churches without free churche.Cosmology: Creation is God's good work; history is linear (creation → fall → redemption → consummation); the world is fallen yet sustained and called to stewardship and renewal under God's providence.
Protestant Churches without free churche.Ecclesiology: Visible, institutional churches with denominational polity (episcopal, presbyterial or connexional forms); the church is both sacramental community and organized body for mission, often with historic ties to national life.
Protestant Churches without free churche.Epistemology: Primacy of Scripture tempered by tradition, reason and experience (e.g., Anglican/Reformed balances); historical-critical scholarship and theological reflection are widely used to interpret doctrine and practice.
Protestant Churches without free churche.Eschatology: Hope in Christ's return, final judgment, resurrection and new creation; emphasis on 'already/not yet' kingdom inaugurated in Christ rather than uniform literalist apocalyptic timelines.
Protestant Churches without free churche.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms are grounded in Scripture, interpreted through tradition and reason; emphasis on love of God and neighbor, social justice and public witness, with denominational diversity on specific moral issues.
Protestant Churches without free churche.Exclusivity: Christ is affirmed as the decisive revelation and means of salvation; many mainline bodies stress evangelism alongside ecumenical openness and pastoral sensitivity about the destiny of non-Christians, resulting in a range from exclusivist to more inclusivist positions.
Protestant Churches without free churche.Metaphysics: Trinitarian theism: one personal, transcendent God (Father, Son, Spirit) who is Creator and sustains reality; spiritual and material realms are real and God acts providentially (sacramental efficacy affirmed to varying degrees).
Protestant Churches without free churche.Praxis: Structured/liturgical public worship with preaching, prayer, sacraments (baptism, Eucharist) and ordained ministry; strong commitment to pastoral care, catechesis, education and organized social ministries.
Protestant Churches without free churche.Soteriology: Salvation is accomplished in Christ and appropriated by faith; justification by faith is central but often understood with nuance (faith enlivened by love, sacraments as means of grace); multiple atonement models coexist in teaching.

Reformed Church in Romania.Anthropology: Humans are made in God's image but corrupted by sin (total depravity in classical Reformed terms); persons remain morally and spiritually responsible and called to life in covenantal relation with God.
Reformed Church in Romania.Cosmology: God created and sustains the cosmos; creation is good but groans after the Fall; providence governs history while God’s kingdom is both present and promised to be consummated.
Reformed Church in Romania.Ecclesiology: Presbyterian-synodal governance with local congregations led by pastors and elders, accountable to regional presbyteries and general synods; church order and confessions guide life and discipline.
Reformed Church in Romania.Epistemology: Sola Scriptura: the Bible is the authoritative norm interpreted by reason, tradition and confessions (e.g., Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession); preaching is primary means of doctrinal formation.
Reformed Church in Romania.Eschatology: Typically Reformed/incarnational—Christ’s return, final judgment, resurrection of the dead and renewal of creation; many hold an amillennial or inaugurated-kingdom perspective rather than literal premillennialism.
Reformed Church in Romania.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms flow from Scripture and the Decalogue interpreted in a covenantal context; emphasizes personal holiness, social responsibility, justice, and stewardship of creation.
Reformed Church in Romania.Exclusivity: Affirms salvation is only through Jesus Christ and proclaims the gospel to all, while also acknowledging doctrines of common grace and God’s sovereign election; fellowship is defined by conformity to Scripture and confessional standards.
Reformed Church in Romania.Metaphysics: Classical theism: one triune, sovereign, personal God who is Creator, immutable and providential; reality is ultimately grounded in God's being and covenant relations as interpreted by Reformed theology.
Reformed Church in Romania.Praxis: Worship centers on preaching of the Word, prayer, psalmody/hymnody and the two sacraments (Baptism and Lord's Supper); strong catechesis, pastoral care and community/social service are important.
Reformed Church in Romania.Soteriology: Salvation is by God’s grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone; emphasizes justification, sanctification, assurance, and the doctrine of election/unconditional predestination within covenantal structure.

Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Anthropology: Humans are body-soul composites made in the image of God (imago Dei), endowed with dignity and free will, wounded by original sin but capable of receiving sanctifying grace and being transformed in virtue toward communion with God and others.
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Cosmology: A created, ordered cosmos sustained by God's providence, populated by spiritual beings (angels), fallen by sin and awaiting teleological restoration in God's kingdom; history moves toward divine consummation.
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Ecclesiology: The Church is One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic: a visible hierarchical communion of bishops in union with the Pope; the Latin Church is the Western (Roman) particular church expressing this unity principally through the Roman Rite.
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Epistemology: Knowledge of God and doctrine rests on Scripture, Apostolic Tradition, and the Magisterium, attended by reason and theological reflection; papal and conciliar infallibility apply in narrowly defined circumstances.
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Eschatology: Affirms particular judgment at death, resurrection of the body, final general judgment, heaven and hell, and purgatory as purification for the saved, culminating in the renewal of creation (new heavens and new earth).
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Ethics & Morality: Moral teaching is grounded in natural law and Divine Revelation; objective moral truths, the Ten Commandments, virtues (cardinal and theological), and Magisterial guidance direct personal and social moral action.
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Exclusivity: Teaches it possesses the fullness of means of salvation and apostolic succession and thus a unique mediatory role, while also acknowledging that non-Catholics and non-Christians may be saved by God's mercy under certain conditions outside visible communion.
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Metaphysics: Classical theism (influenced by Aristotelian-Thomistic realism): God is the necessary, personal Creator; created beings have real essences; reality is ordered and purposeful; sacraments effect real, objective grace (e.g., Eucharistic doctrine of transubstantiation).
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Praxis: Centered on the sacramental and liturgical life (especially the Mass/Eucharist) and the seven sacraments, plus prayer, sacramental confession, liturgical calendar observances, devotional practices, and works of charity and mercy.
Roman Catholic; Latin Church;.Soteriology: Salvation is accomplished uniquely in Christ's life, death, and resurrection and applied by grace through faith, baptism, the sacraments, and human cooperation (sanctification and infused righteousness); merits are possible only by grace.

Russian Orthodox Church.Anthropology: Humans are created in the image and likeness of God, fallen into sin but retaining freedom and the capacity for restoration. The goal is deification (theosis): restoration of the likeness through participation in divine life.
Russian Orthodox Church.Cosmology: A created, ordered cosmos sustained by God and populated by visible and invisible beings (angels/demons). The material world is essentially good but fallen and sacramentally permeable to divine grace.
Russian Orthodox Church.Ecclesiology: The Church is the Body of Christ, apostolic and sacramental, possessing continuity through apostolic succession and conciliar (soborny) governance. The Russian Orthodox Church sees itself as part of the one Orthodox Church under episcopal authority and synods.
Russian Orthodox Church.Epistemology: Knowledge of God is mediated by Divine Revelation (Scripture and Holy Tradition), validated by patristic consensus and the Church’s liturgical-theological experience; contemplative prayer (theoria) is privileged for direct experiential knowledge.
Russian Orthodox Church.Eschatology: Belief in Christ’s second coming, the resurrection of the dead, final judgment, and the renewal of creation (new heavens and new earth). Emphasis on participation in Christ’s life now as preparation; prayers for the departed and expectation of restorative consummation.
Russian Orthodox Church.Ethics & Morality: A virtue-centered ethic aimed at loving communion with God and neighbor. Moral life is shaped by commandments, virtues (humility, charity), liturgical rhythm, and ascetic practices rather than primarily legalistic rules.
Russian Orthodox Church.Exclusivity: Maintains that the fullness of truth and means of salvation subsist in the Orthodox Church, while entrusting ultimate judgment to God and recognizing God's mercy beyond visible boundaries; ecumenical engagement is cautious and often guarded.
Russian Orthodox Church.Metaphysics: Monotheistic Trinitarianism: one God in three Persons. Reality is grounded in the uncreated God whose divine 'essence' is transcendent while His 'energies' are communicable, enabling real union with creatures.
Russian Orthodox Church.Praxis: Liturgy and sacraments (Baptism, Eucharist, Chrismation, Confession, Marriage, Ordination, Unction), daily and communal prayer, fasting, veneration of icons, almsgiving, and monasticism as primary modes of spiritual life.
Russian Orthodox Church.Soteriology: Salvation is transformative union with God (theosis) accomplished by Christ’s incarnation, death, and resurrection and effected by divine grace working in synergy with human repentance, faith, prayer, sacraments, and ascetic struggle.

Serbian Orthodox Church.Anthropology: Humans are created in the image of God (ikon), fallen by sin but capable of restoration; personhood is relational and meant for union with God through grace and community.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Cosmology: Creation is intentionally good, made by God and sustained by Him; the material world is a theater for divine-human communion and theosis, not intrinsically evil but fallen and to be redeemed.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Ecclesiology: The Serbian Orthodox Church is an autocephalous Eastern Orthodox Church governed by bishops in apostolic succession and led by a patriarch; the Church is the sacramental Body of Christ where truth and salvation are mediated.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Epistemology: Knowledge of God is chiefly revelatory and experiential: Scripture, Holy Tradition (fathers, councils, liturgy) and mystical theology (hesychasm/apophaticism) provide authoritative knowing over purely rational proofs.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Eschatology: Affirms Christ's return, general resurrection, final judgment and new creation; emphasis on participation in eternal life (theosis) rather than speculative chronology, with hope for transformation of persons and cosmos.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Ethics & Morality: Moral life centers on theosis-expressing virtues (love, humility, repentance, sobriety); moral norms arise from Scripture, patristic tradition and liturgical formation, emphasizing communal responsibility and ascetic practice.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Exclusivity: Maintains that full means of salvation subsist in the Orthodox Church and its sacraments; recognizes genuine elements of truth in other Christian traditions but regards canonical Orthodoxy as the normative path to fullness of life in Christ.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Metaphysics: Trinitarian theism grounded in Eastern Orthodox theology: one God in three Persons; reality participates in God's energies; emphasis on sacramental and iconographic realism rather than radical dualism.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Praxis: Liturgical and sacramental life is primary: Divine Liturgy, Eucharist, Baptism, Chrismation, Confession, fasting, prayer, veneration of icons, monasticism and pastoral rites shape belief and life.
Serbian Orthodox Church.Soteriology: Salvation is therapeutic deification (theosis): healing and restoration of the whole person through Christ, enacted by the Church's sacraments, repentance, prayer and ascetic struggle in synergy with divine grace.

Seventh-day Adventist Church.Anthropology: Humans are created in God's image, fallen by sin, and are mortal rather than intrinsically immortal. Death is a state of unconscious 'sleep' until the resurrection; personal responsibility and freedom of choice are emphasized.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Cosmology: Affirms divine creation (typically understood as six literal days in official teaching) and rejects evolutionary naturalism; the cosmos is understood within the Great Controversy narrative explaining the origin and presence of evil.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Ecclesiology: A denominational, representative polity (local churches, conferences, unions, divisions, General Conference) combining ordained ministry with strong lay participation; institutions (schools, hospitals, publishing) are central to identity and mission.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Epistemology: The Bible is the final authority (the church's sole creed); Ellen G. White's writings are viewed as a prophetic, authoritative but subordinate and testable source of guidance. Interpretation uses a historicist approach to prophecy and integrates Scripture with reason, experience and tradition.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Eschatology: Historicist and premillennial: belief in an imminent, visible Second Coming of Christ, an investigative judgment prior to that event, a millennium (the righteous in heaven), final destruction or annihilation of the wicked, and a renewed earth and new creation; prophetic emphasis on Daniel and Revelation.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Ethics & Morality: Morality is grounded in the Ten Commandments and New Testament teaching; the church emphasizes healthful living (diet, temperance), family and sexual ethics (sexual relations reserved for heterosexual marriage), stewardship, service and social responsibility.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Exclusivity: Affirms that salvation is possible only through Jesus Christ and proclaims Adventist end‑time teachings as a final message for the world; at the same time it recognizes other Christians as fellow believers and often cooperates with them in mission and service.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Metaphysics: Trinitarian theism: one God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) who is Creator, Redeemer and Sustainer; reality includes physical and spiritual realms (angels/demons). Moral reality is framed by the 'Great Controversy' between Christ and Satan; humans have free will and the moral law (Ten Commandments) expresses God's character.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Praxis: Sabbath (Saturday) worship and rest, Bible study, prayer meetings, baptism by immersion, Lord's Supper and foot‑washing, active evangelism and missionary work, extensive educational and medical institutions, and practice of tithing and lay ministry.
Seventh-day Adventist Church.Soteriology: Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, with righteousness imputed and sanctification as ongoing transformation. Distinctive doctrines include the investigative judgment (a pre‑advent review of records) and the expectation that obedient living (fruit of faith, including Sabbath observance) accompanies true conversion.

Shia.Anthropology: Humans are created with fitrah (innate disposition) and reason ('aql), endowed with moral responsibility and relative free will; the soul is accountable and capable of moral growth under guidance from scripture and the Imams.
Shia.Cosmology: The universe is a created order of God populated by humans, angels and jinn; in mainstream Shia it is a moral arena under divine providence, while some mystical/Ismaili currents articulate layered or emanative cosmologies.
Shia.Ecclesiology: Centering on the doctrine of the Imamate (divinely appointed leadership); in Twelver and Ismaili forms Imams are central and often infallible; during the occultation authority is exercised by jurists, while Zaydi and other branches have different, less centralized structures.
Shia.Epistemology: Authoritative sources are the Quran, hadith—especially those transmitted by the Ahl al‑Bayt—reason ('aql) and ijtihad; interpretive authority resides in the Imams and, in their absence, qualified jurists (mujtahids/maraji').
Shia.Eschatology: Affirms resurrection, judgment and eschatological reward/punishment; highlights the return of the Mahdi (the Hidden/last Imam) who will establish justice; martyrdom (notably Karbala) figures prominently in redemptive narrative.
Shia.Ethics & Morality: Ethics center on justice, opposition to oppression, piety, loyalty and communal responsibility; moral norms are developed from scripture, hadith of the Prophet’s family, and juristic reasoning.
Shia.Exclusivity: Claims exclusive legitimacy for the leadership and authoritative interpretation vested in the Ahl al‑Bayt and their rightful successors, though salvation is not typically portrayed as limited solely to sect members; views on other Muslims vary by school and context.
Shia.Metaphysics: Absolute, transcendent monotheism (tawhid) with an emphasis on divine justice ('adl); God is wholly other but knowable through names, scripture and divinely‑appointed guides; Imams are seen (especially in Twelver and Ismaili thought) as possessing special spiritual authority and knowledge.
Shia.Praxis: Follows the Five Pillars with distinctive Shia forms (e.g., Ja'fari jurisprudence, combining prayers, use of a turbah, observance of Ashura), additional practices like khums and shrine visitation, and clerically mediated religious life.
Shia.Soteriology: Salvation rests on faith, righteous deeds, repentance, adherence to the Quran and the guidance of the Ahl al‑Bayt; intercession by the Imams and God’s mercy are important, and social justice is integral to salvific life.

Sikhism.Anthropology: Humans are embodied souls whose spiritual ignorance, ego (haumai) and attachment to maya bind them to the cycle of rebirth; they possess the capacity for divine remembrance and moral transformation.
Sikhism.Cosmology: The universe is created and sustained by God's Hukam; existence unfolds under divine order, with human life occurring within cyclical processes influenced by karma—no detailed mythic cosmogony but emphasis on God's continuous governance and immanence.
Sikhism.Ecclesiology: Community-centered (sangat) worship organized around the Gurdwara and the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru; no hereditary priesthood—granthis and institutions (e.g., Akal Takht) serve communal, liturgical and legal functions; the Khalsa provides a pan-Sikh disciplinary identity.
Sikhism.Epistemology: Spiritual knowledge is received through the Gurus' revelation preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib and verified by direct mystical experience and ethical living; reason and practice are measured against scripture and the community, while mere ritual is insufficient.
Sikhism.Eschatology: No elaborate apocalyptic doctrine: emphasis is on liberation from the cycle of birth and death (samsara) through mukti; the final state is union with God rather than detailed afterlife cosmography.
Sikhism.Ethics & Morality: Core duties: truthful living (sat), honest work (kirat karni), sharing (vand chakna), equality, humility and selfless service (seva); rejects caste-based discrimination and empty ritualism.
Sikhism.Exclusivity: Generally inclusive and universalist about God's accessibility—acknowledges truth in other religions—while maintaining a distinct communal, ethical and ritual identity (notably the Khalsa); salvation is not limited to a single social group.
Sikhism.Metaphysics: Strict monotheism (Ik Onkar): one God (Waheguru) who is both transcendent (nirgun) and immanent (sargun), timeless, creator and ground of being; reality ordered by divine will (Hukam).
Sikhism.Praxis: Regular naam-simran (recitation/meditation on God's name), kirtan (devotional singing), ardas (prayer), participation in sangats at the gurdwara, langar (communal kitchen), seva, and voluntary initiation (Amrit) for the Khalsa.
Sikhism.Soteriology: Liberation (mukti) is attained through God's grace combined with devotion (Naam), ethical living, meditation, and community discipline; jivan-mukti (realization while alive) is an ideal—ultimate aim is experiential union with God.

Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Anthropology: Humans are body-soul persons made in the image and likeness of God, fallen but redeemable; true human fullness is realized in communal participation in divine life (deification) through grace and cooperation.
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Cosmology: The created world is essentially good, inhabited by angels and subject to corruption by sin; creation is a sacramental theater for God’s presence and will be restored in the eschaton.
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Ecclesiology: A sui iuris Eastern Catholic Church in full communion with the Bishop of Rome; governed by bishops and synodal structures, rooted in apostolic succession and sacramental life while preserving Byzantine patrimony.
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Epistemology: Knowledge of God is mediated by Revelation—Scripture and Holy Tradition—read through the Fathers, liturgy, prayerful experience, and theological reflection within the living Church.
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Eschatology: Focus on resurrection, final judgment, and the restoration/transformation of creation; eternal communion with God (full deification) is the goal, with postmortem purification understood more as therapeutic healing than purely juridical punishment.
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Ethics & Morality: Moral teaching flows from Gospel virtues, the commandments, and ascetic practice; emphasis on repentance, humility, love, charity, communal responsibility and liturgical formation of moral life.
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Exclusivity: Affirms its membership in the one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church in communion with Rome and the normative role of its sacramental life for believers, while recognizing that God’s saving will can operate beyond visible institutional boundaries.
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Metaphysics: Classical Christian theism: one Triune God; Christ is fully divine and fully human; reality is ordered toward communion with God and the sacraments disclose and transmit divine life (theosis).
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Praxis: Byzantine Rite liturgy (Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom), sacramental life (Baptism/Chrismation/Eucharist, Confession, Marriage, Orders, Anointing), icon veneration, fasts, liturgical calendar, and monastic/pastoral practices (vernacular and Church Slavonic usage).
Slovak Greek Catholic Church.Soteriology: Salvation is primarily healing and deification (theosis) effected by Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection and by participation in the Mysteries, prayer, repentance, and ascetic discipline (synergy of grace and free response).

Spiritism.Anthropology: Humans are composite beings (spirit + perispirit + body). Personality and moral traits persist after death and are shaped across successive incarnations that advance intellectual and moral development.
Spiritism.Cosmology: The universe is governed by spiritual laws and comprises multiple planes or spheres inhabited by spirits of varying degrees of purification. Worlds and spirits evolve progressively; matter and spirit interact according to moral and natural laws.
Spiritism.Ecclesiology: Non-hierarchical and lay-led: no formal clergy or sacraments. Organization occurs through Spiritist centres, federations, study groups and charities that focus on teaching, practice, and mutual aid.
Spiritism.Epistemology: Knowledge is sought by combining reason, observation/experiment, and mediumistic testimony subject to critical testing. Authenticity is judged by consistency, moral coherence, reproducibility, and rational analysis (Kardec’s critical method).
Spiritism.Eschatology: After death spirits persist and inhabit spheres appropriate to their moral state; purification and progress continue through intermediate states and reincarnations. There is no doctrine of eternal reward/punishment—correction and advancement are central.
Spiritism.Ethics & Morality: Ethics center on universal principles—charity, humility, justice, benevolence—and responsibility for actions. Moral law operates like cause and effect (karma-like): deeds produce appropriate consequences fostering reform.
Spiritism.Exclusivity: Not exclusive or dogmatic: presents itself as a scientific-religious-philosophical inquiry open to verification, affirms truths in other faiths, and encourages free, comparative investigation rather than claiming sole access to truth.
Spiritism.Metaphysics: Monotheistic and dual-aspect: God is the Supreme Intelligence and First Cause; reality includes a material world and an invisible spiritual world of individualized spirits. Humans possess an immortal spirit, a semi-material perispirit, and a transient physical body.
Spiritism.Praxis: Practices include mediumship and controlled communication with spirits, study groups, moral instruction, spiritual healing (passes), philanthropy, and empirical investigation conducted in Spiritist centres and societies.
Spiritism.Soteriology: Salvation equals gradual moral and intellectual perfection achieved through self-improvement, repentance, charity, and successive reincarnations. Liberation from error and suffering results from learning and moral reform rather than punitive eternal damnation.

Sunni.Anthropology: Humans are created beings made from clay with a fitrah (innate disposition) toward God, endowed with reason and moral responsibility; the soul (nafs/ruh) is accountable, with debate within Sunni thought about the scope of free will under divine decree.
Sunni.Cosmology: The universe is a created, purposeful order brought into being by God, containing visible and unseen realms (angels, jinn); natural phenomena are signs (ayat) of divine wisdom and sovereignty.
Sunni.Ecclesiology: No single hierarchical church; authority rests with qualified scholars (ulama), jurists and local imams and with four main Sunni legal schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) providing organizational and interpretive cohesion for the ummah.
Sunni.Epistemology: Knowledge is rooted in revelation (Qur'an and authenticated hadith), with reason used to interpret texts; legal and theological methods employ consensus (ijma), analogy (qiyas) and established hadith criticism to determine religious truth.
Sunni.Eschatology: Affirms bodily resurrection, a final Day of Judgment, accountability, reward in Paradise (Jannah) and punishment in Hell (Jahannam), with signs of the Hour and the role of prophets and intercession in the eschaton.
Sunni.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms derive primarily from the Qur'an and Sunnah and are elaborated by Sharia; virtues like justice, charity, honesty and communal responsibility are emphasized alongside clear prohibitions.
Sunni.Exclusivity: Claims to represent mainstream orthodox Islam and defines core boundaries around Tawhid and acceptance of Muhammad as God’s final prophet; it is generally inclusive of Sunni legal and theological diversity but distinguishes itself from non-Sunni interpretations (e.g., some Shia, heterodox movements) while attitudes toward other Muslims vary by context.
Sunni.Metaphysics: Affirms strict monotheism (Tawhid): one transcendent, personal God (Allah) who is the creator and sustainer, with revealed attributes affirmed without anthropomorphism; reality includes angels, prophets, scripture and divine decree (qadar) as central metaphysical truths.
Sunni.Praxis: Religious life centers on the Five Pillars (shahada, prayer, almsgiving, fasting, pilgrimage), regular ritual worship, mosque-centered communal life, and adherence to fiqh (jurisprudential) rulings from the recognized madhhabs.
Sunni.Soteriology: Salvation rests on faith (iman) in God and His prophets accompanied by righteous deeds, repentance, and reliance on God’s mercy; adherence to scripture and prophetic example is decisive for ultimate judgment.

Taoism (Han Chinese).Anthropology: Humans are embodied agents of qi whose original nature is spontaneous simplicity (ziran) and alignment with the Tao; ignorance, desire, and social conditioning obscure that nature but can be transformed by cultivation.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Cosmology: The cosmos is a living, cyclic process: the Tao manifests into yin-yang and wuxing (five phases), qi circulates through heaven, earth, and humans, and patterns of harmony or disharmony determine cosmic and social order.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Ecclesiology: Religious Taoism comprises organized lineages and schools (e.g., Celestial Masters, Quanzhen), temple networks and priesthoods alongside lay communities; institutional forms are syncretic and locally rooted.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Epistemology: Knowledge is primarily experiential and intuitive (non‑conceptual attunement to the Tao) verified by embodied practice; scriptures (Daodejing, Zhuangzi, Daozang) and paradoxical teaching devices guide but do not replace lived realization.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Eschatology: No single linear end-time doctrine; emphasis is on cycles, transformation, and personal/collective renewal; some sects include apocalyptic or millenarian elements, while mainstream focuses on immortalization and ongoing cosmic harmonization.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Ethics & Morality: Ethics emphasize wu-wei (non‑forcing), naturalness, humility, non-contention, and compassion; moral guidance is pragmatic and context-sensitive rather than rule‑bound, privileging attunement to the flow of circumstances.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Exclusivity: Generally non‑exclusive and highly syncretic: Taoist practice commonly coexists with Buddhism, Confucianism, and Chinese folk religion rather than demanding exclusive adherence.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Metaphysics: Central is the Tao (Dao) — an ineffable, immanent-and-transcendent ground/principle from which all arises; reality is constituted by qi and the dynamic interplay of yin-yang and five phases rather than fixed substances.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Praxis: A wide repertoire: meditation, breath-work, qigong/Tai Chi, inner (neidan) and external (waidan) alchemy, ritual, talismans, liturgy, confession and exorcism, moral self-cultivation, and community rites performed by priests/masters.
Taoism (Han Chinese).Soteriology: Salvation is restoration to harmony with the Tao — realized as ethical spontaneity, longevity or spiritual transcendence (immortality/xian), inner liberation from suffering and social constraints through cultivation, ritual, or alchemy.

The African Church.Summary: Do you mean a specific denomination called "The African Church" (the African-initiated Anglican-style denomination founded in Nigeria, 1901), or do you mean "African Christianity" or "African Independent Churches" more broadly? Which should I describe?

United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Anthropology: Humans created in the image of God, endowed with dignity and vocation; the Fall introduced sin, corruption and alienation from God, so humanity is morally responsible yet in need of redemption.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Cosmology: Affirms creation ex nihilo by God; the universe is intentionally ordered and sustained by divine providence, with both material and spiritual dimensions interacting in history.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Ecclesiology: Local congregations led by ordained pastors and elders with an emphasis on mission and evangelism; congregational accountability, discipline and active lay participation are typical, aiming for unity in essentials and liberty in non-essentials.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Epistemology: Scripture is the supreme authority (sola scriptura), interpreted through preaching, prayer and the guidance of the Holy Spirit; reason and personal experience are secondary and subordinate to the Bible.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Eschatology: Affirms the future bodily return of Christ, resurrection, final judgment and eternal destinies (heaven and hell); many adherents hold imminent-return and historic evangelical perspectives, stressing readiness and missionary urgency.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Ethics & Morality: Moral norms are grounded in the Bible; emphasis on personal holiness, family and sexual ethics, social responsibility, compassion for the poor, and ethical transformation as evidence of faith.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Exclusivity: Maintains that Jesus Christ is the sole means of salvation and endorses active evangelism; this exclusivist claim is commonly coupled with calls to respectful witness and pastoral care for nonbelievers.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Metaphysics: Classical theism: one personal God revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit; God is transcendent and immanent, sovereign, omnipotent and moral; spiritual realities (angels, demons) are real and active.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Praxis: Worship centers on Bible-based preaching, prayer and congregational singing; common practices include baptism (typically believer's baptism) and the Lord's Supper, evangelism, discipleship, prayer meetings, healing ministries and community engagement.
United Evangelical Church—in Nigeria.Soteriology: Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ alone, secured by his atoning death and resurrection; requires repentance and new birth, with assurance of salvation available to believers.

Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Anthropology: Personhood is relational and continuous across generations; identity is rooted in lineage and kinship, with the family as the primary moral and social unit.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Cosmology: A layered cosmos (heaven, earth, underworld) governed by balances (yin-yang, harmony) with powerful local deities and spirit presences; time is cyclic and tied to agricultural seasons and festival cycles.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Ecclesiology: Decentralized and household-centered; authority rests with family heads, village institutions (đình, miếu) and various ritual specialists (thầy cúng, đạo Mẫu priests), not a single centralized church.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Epistemology: Knowledge is transmitted orally and ritually through elders, family memory, and ritual specialists; dreams, signs, and the practical efficacy of rites validate belief.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Eschatology: The dead continue as ancestral spirits whose welfare depends on offerings; neglected spirits may become restless; ideas about rebirth or merit vary and are syncretically blended with Buddhist notions.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Ethics & Morality: Filial piety (hiếu), respect for elders, reciprocity, and preservation of family honor are central; moral conduct is oriented toward sustaining social and ancestral harmony.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Exclusivity: Generally non‑exclusive and highly syncretic—coexists with Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism, local cults, and even Christianity; practice is defined by kinship and local belonging rather than doctrinal commitment.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Metaphysics: Ancestors' souls (hồn) and local spirits are real and immanent; the household altar mediates ongoing reciprocal relations between the living and the dead, and spiritual forces influence daily fortune and misfortune.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Praxis: Household altars, daily incense and offerings, death-anniversary rites (giỗ), Tết rituals, tomb-sweeping, votive paper burning, and occasional use of mediums or divination; community rites occur at village temples and communal houses.
Vietnam Ancestral worshipping / Traditio.Soteriology: Not focused on individual salvation but on maintaining harmony, prosperity, and peace for both living and ancestors; proper ritual upkeep secures ancestral favor and averts calamity.

Vodou.Anthropology: Persons are composite (body plus soul components) defined by kinship, community roles and reciprocal relations with lwa and ancestors; identity is social and relational rather than atomized.
Vodou.Cosmology: A connected cosmos of the visible world, the spirit realm (often called Ginen/ancestral domain) and the transcendent creator; lwa mediate between humans and the creator and move freely between realms.
Vodou.Ecclesiology: Decentralized, kin- and lineage-based congregations (hounfour/peristyles) led by houngans/mambos and councils; authority is local and charismatic rather than centralized.
Vodou.Epistemology: Knowledge is revealed experientially via spirit communication, dreams, possession, divination and initiatory transmission; oral tradition and ritual efficacy are primary validators of truth.
Vodou.Eschatology: Limited focus on final ends; emphasis on ancestors, continuing influence of the dead, possible return/rebirth motifs and ongoing reciprocal relations between living and dead.
Vodou.Ethics & Morality: Morality emphasizes reciprocity, respect, obligation to family and spirits, communal responsibility and the avoidance of taboos; ethical norms are enforced by community and spirit sanctions rather than abstract law.
Vodou.Exclusivity: Generally non‑exclusive and highly syncretic (commonly coexisting with Catholic practices); membership is flexible and Vodou rarely demands sole religious allegiance.
Vodou.Metaphysics: A layered spiritual realism: a distant creator (Bondye) and a populated world of lwa (spirits), ancestors and forces that interact with material reality; humans possess multiple soul aspects and vital forces.
Vodou.Praxis: Ritual life centers on services (servis), drumming, singing, dance, offerings, altars, possession trance, divination and initiation (e.g., kanzo); priests (houngan) and priestesses (mambo) and congregation maintain practice.
Vodou.Soteriology: Not oriented to individual eternal salvation but to practical restoration: protection, healing, equilibrium, social harmony and redress of misfortune through ritual and spirit assistance.

Yiguandao.Anthropology: Human beings are inherently connected to the primordial Mother but have fallen into ignorance and entanglement with worldly desires and karmic causes; persons possess a spiritual core that can be recovered.
Yiguandao.Cosmology: Syncretic cyclical cosmos in which spirits undergo cycles of birth and rebirth under karmic bondage; history moves toward a period of cosmic renewal in which the Mother dispenses salvation through revealed messengers and rites.
Yiguandao.Ecclesiology: Organized, hierarchical movement with temples, ordained leaders and transmission lineages; highly missionary and networked, with local branches and centralized authorities differing by region and sect.
Yiguandao.Epistemology: Authority rests on revelatory experience and spirit-writing, charismatic masters and lineage transmission, validated by ritual efficacy and moral transformation; scriptures and oral teachings produced through purported spiritual communication are central sources of knowledge.
Yiguandao.Eschatology: Millenarian-tinged expectation of imminent cosmic salvation and renewal administered by the Mother and her emissaries; establishment of a restored moral order and liberation for adherents are anticipated outcomes.
Yiguandao.Ethics & Morality: Emphasis on moral self-cultivation: filial piety, compassion, honesty, charity, abstention from harmful habits; ethical conduct is treated as necessary evidence of inner transformation and a condition for salvation.
Yiguandao.Exclusivity: Generally universalistic and syncretic—asserts a unique salvific program but often welcomes converts from diverse backgrounds; some branches emphasize the movement as the sole authentic path while others are more inclusive and pluralistic.
Yiguandao.Metaphysics: Monistic-soteriological: a transcendent, primordial deity (often conceived as the Unborn Venerable Mother) is the source of all beings; the world and selves are manifestations that can be returned to that source through spiritual restoration.
Yiguandao.Praxis: Ritual repertoire includes communal worship, recitation of scriptures and salvation texts, repentance ceremonies, spirit-writing-derived revelations, ordination/lineage transmission, proselytizing and periodic purification practices (fasts, vegetarian observance in some groups).
Yiguandao.Soteriology: Salvation is restoration to the Mother through faith, repentance, moral reform, ritual participation and receiving transmitted teachings/rites; redemption is communal and practical, removing karmic burden and achieving release from cyclical rebirth.

Zion Christian Church.Anthropology: Humans are embodied spiritual beings created by God, vulnerable to sickness, sin and spiritual attack; community, ritual cleansing and pastoral care restore spiritual and social harmony.
Zion Christian Church.Cosmology: The world is created and sustained by God but populated by visible and invisible beings; earthly events reflect interactions between divine will, ancestral influence and human action.
Zion Christian Church.Ecclesiology: A hierarchical, centralized African-initiated church organized under a prophetic leader and regional officials; strong corporate identity expressed through uniforms, emblems, disciplinary structures and active lay roles.
Zion Christian Church.Epistemology: Authority rests on the Bible plus prophetic revelation, dreams, visions and the pronouncements of church leaders; experiential confirmation (healing, prophecy) is a key test of truth.
Zion Christian Church.Eschatology: Rooted in mainstream Christian expectations of Christ's return, final judgment and resurrection, the emphasis is on moral preparedness and present experience of God's kingdom through healing and deliverance.
Zion Christian Church.Ethics & Morality: Ethics stress communal responsibility, respect for elders and leaders, sexual fidelity, sobriety, honesty and rejection of occult practices; moral conduct is tied to spiritual protection and blessing.
Zion Christian Church.Exclusivity: Open to diverse ethnicities and syncretic in practice, the ZCC nevertheless claims distinctive spiritual authority and ritual means of grace; membership and obedience to its structures are seen as the normal route to its promised benefits.
Zion Christian Church.Metaphysics: Monotheistic Christian belief in one God and Jesus Christ alongside a vivid spiritual realm of angels, demons and ancestors; spiritual forces tangibly affect health and fortune and may be mediated by sacraments and ritual objects.
Zion Christian Church.Praxis: Worship includes weekly services with prophetic preaching, singing, dancing, laying on of hands, use of holy water/ashes/emblems, prayer camps and annual pilgrimages to the movement's Zion (Moria) for healing and renewal.
Zion Christian Church.Soteriology: Salvation centers on Jesus (faith and repentance) but is lived out communally through healing, deliverance, sanctification and obedience to church rites and leadership; divine healing and protection are emphasized.
